articles.title: [DECODED] AI is changing our lives more than we realize
articles.summary: AI is reshaping our lives more than we realize, from how much time we spend online, to how safe our children are, to how we vote

blocks.text: AI is reshaping our lives more than we realize, from how much time we spend online, to how safe our children are, to how we vote

items: Filipinos spend an average of 36 hours and 12 minutes online weekly, significantly higher than the global average of 19 hours, with a notable usage of generative AI tools.

Concerns about child online safety have intensified, prompting discussions among stakeholders, including Meta, about the effectiveness of safety features and the responsibility of platforms in managing harmful content.
The upcoming Social Good Summit will focus on the impact of AI on society, emphasizing the need for human values and community involvement in guiding technological changes.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

How much time do you spend online in a week? I checked mine using the Screen Time feature on my devices, and found that I spent around 60 hours last week on apps related to productivity, social, and entertainment. But that’s mostly because my work requires a lot of time to be connected to the internet — or so I convince myself to feel less guilty about my high screen time.

Media intelligence company Meltwater and creative agency We Are Social have released Digital 2027, their latest installment in their annual reports that provide data on digital trends worldwide, including social media use and the adoption of AI tools.

Their latest report showed that Filipinos lead in social media and online video time, averaging 36 hours and 12 minutes a week, across the over 230 countries and territories included in the report. That’s nearly double the global average of about 19 hours.

Filipinos are also among the most active users of generative AI in the world, with 94.4% saying they use AI tools monthly and 54.6% saying they used ChatGPT in the past month. These numbers are both higher than the global averages of 85.2% and 34.7%, respectively.

The numbers in the Digital 2027 report only cover users aged 16 and above. But recent incidents have shown that children, among the most vulnerable, also spend a lot of time on online platforms — so much so that debates about banning or limiting their screen time have become more urgent than ever.

I attended an event hosted by Meta last week. The company brought together representatives from government, civil society, and the technology sector to discuss child online safety and help young people and their parents to recognize online risks — especially after multiple incidents of school violence were reported nationwide.

Meta’s response to child safety rests on safety features, like age verification and parental controls. But these tools, while they are helpful, leave much of the burden on children and parents rather than on the platforms that host and profit from the content users are expected to always scrutinize. They can even be circumvented.

As a result, harmful content still slips through — which AI can now generate in seconds. We saw this recently in Brazil’s 2026 general election, where the surge of AI-generated content bypassed Brazil’s electoral rules.

A report from fact-checking agency Agência Lupa said that, of the AI-generated political content they monitored, about 60% were deepfakes and lacked transparency labels. Although regulations banning deepfakes and requiring disclosure for AI content were in place, these were “fully and truly disrespected by all stakeholders,” said Agência Lupa founder Cristina Tardáguila.

These things tell us one thing: AI is reshaping our lives more than we realize, from how much time we spend online, to how safe our children are, to how we vote. What we must ensure now is that we, the humans, are the ones guiding this change.

That is the conversation we’ll be having at Rappler’s Social Good Summit on November 21. This year’s theme is “We, The Humans,” because we will put human values, creativity, and community at the center of the conversation as we tackle the harms posed by unregulated and abused AI.

The summit will feature the world’s foremost AI experts, such as Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa, historian Yuval Noah Harari (pre-recorded), human rights activist Agnès Callamard, Nobel Committee Chair Jørgen Watne Frydnes, and AI Singapore’s Leslie Teo. The full list of speakers is available here.
Explore: Social Good Summit 2026: We, The Humans

Participants can also choose two out of the six exclusive masterclasses that will take place throughout the day. The topics range from privacy in the age of AI agents, to vibe coding lessons, editorial cartooning, crisis management, and data-driven storytelling — which I will facilitate alongside my colleague Kit Posadas.

blocks.text: American voters have inflicted a generational defeat on the Republican Party in the midterm elections, with Democrats winning control of both houses of Congress: the House of Representatives and Senate.

Donald Trump’s party has been defeated in states where it hadn’t lost for a generation — or longer: Texas, South Carolina and Kansas. These have been red states for quite some time, but this shows the Republicans are really suffering in their own heartland.

While Democrats were widely predicted to take the House and had a reasonable chance to win the Senate, no one could have predicted at the beginning of 2026 such a huge “blue wave” washing over the US by November.

In fact, Republicans barely held on in Senate races in Louisiana and Florida — states that have long been firmly red — and the race in Mississippi will go down to the wire. And Democrats held on everywhere that was contested: in most cases, it wasn’t even close.

One of the very significant lessons from the Democrats’ crushing victory is the party’s ability to accommodate a broad church of candidates and ideas. For example, Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim socialist, won a Senate seat in Michigan, while Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, won in Kansas.

Even though there’s been a lot of heartache and internal wrangling for the Democrats about left versus centre politics, this just shows that when they win by a big enough margin there’s room for everybody in the party.
This means the Senate and House will look very different from the way they looked before the midterms.

And the message for the Republicans? This is unquestionably a repudiation of Trump, and this is backed up by his record-low approval ratings, and the fact that four in 10 voters in exit polls said they were motivated to send a message to the sitting president.
He has launched one of the most unpopular wars in American history in Iran, which has had direct effects on people’s lives and livelihoods, raising the cost of living for everyone.

And while he has typically distanced himself from any responsibility for the election result, there is no question the way Americans feel about the economy is very closely linked to the way they feel about Trump. And this is a decisive repudiation.
It will take longer to see the effect on Trumpism or the MAGA movement.

The question is, after such a loss, will his grip on the Republican Party now loosen? He’s not going to be on the ballot again – no matter what he might say – so he’ll be a lame duck president. So the question is: will this result make Republicans turn away from Trump?

They will have some serious considerations: what if inflation is still high in 2028, or the Iran War is still going? The results of the presidential election could be even more devastating for Republicans.

Another interesting aspect of the midterms result is that the Democrats successfully took the focus off all the issues Republicans have seen as winners in recent years, such as the culture wars (in particular trans issues) and immigration.
In this election, nothing compared to cost of living, especially when people could see direct links between Trump’s policies and their bills.
Trump has no choice but to accept the result. When a party loses by a really large margin, there’s no way of contesting the results.
He’s made some contradictory comments about how he might respond: he has both threatened to be “Mr Veto”, but also said he can work with the Democrats.

It’s much more likely he will not be able to advance his legislative agenda any further. As president, he can make executive orders and has some foreign policy levers at his disposal, but there will be very real limits on what he can do. He is also likely to be impeached for a third time.

It’ll be interesting to see how serious the Democrats are about ending the Iran war. If they have the political will, they could now threaten to hold up defence spending or shut down the government to try to force a genuine peace deal.
But extricating the US from this war is not a simple matter, given how committed it is at this point.

In general, Republicans will see this as a very serious warning for the 2028 elections. There are some races they could have lost this year and didn’t. If the public mood is the same in 2028 as it is now, the Republicans are in for an even worse defeat.

The Democrats, on the other hand, will see themselves as having a very real chance of taking back the presidency in 2028. One of the big midterm winners was Jon Ossoff, a young Jewish senator from Georgia whose race was called almost immediately after the polls closed. Georgia voted for Trump in 2024.

Ossoff is popular in all parts of the Democratic Party. With his re-election, he has shown he is a compelling speaker who can win in Trump country. He’s the Democrat whose profile has been boosted the most in these midterms, and he’ll certainly be one to watch in 2028, as will Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who was re-elected to the House for a fifth term and is still only 37.
This shows there are real limits to the Trump style of politics in democracies – the relentlessly attention-seeking, culture-warring, crude, and never apologising style of politics.
In the end, real issues that genuinely affect people’s lives will make themselves known, and there’s no way of avoiding that.
David Smith is an Associate Professor in American Politics and Foreign Policy at the US Studies Centre, University of Sydney.

articles.summary: 'There is a policy gap as regards the possible sanction on a member of the Senate with prolonged unauthorized absence rendering them unable to participate in major legislative functions,' the senator…

blocks.text: SOTTO. Senator Tito Sotto speaks during the plenary session on May 12, 2026.
Senate Social Media Unit

'There is a policy gap as regards the possible sanction on a member of the Senate with prolonged unauthorized absence rendering them unable to participate in major legislative functions,' the senator says in his proposed resolution

MANILA, Philippines – Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III has filed proposed Senate Resolution No. 751, seeking clear and institutionalized rules on absenteeism in the upper chamber, amid the prolonged absence of some senators.
Sotto, chairperson of the Senate committee on ethics, cited previous complaints that were referred to his committee, saying there is no provision in the Senate rules on how to resolve the issue.

“There is a policy gap as regards the possible sanction on a member of the Senate with prolonged unauthorized absence rendering them unable to participate in major legislative functions,” the proposed resolution reads.

Under the proposed resolution, Sotto also wants to revisit the rules and “study the best possible approach as regards the issue of prolonged unauthorized absence of senators with the view of ensuring highest standards of public service commensurate to the trust reposed by the electorate.”

“Now, therefore, be it resolved, as it hereby resolved by the Senate of the Philippines, to recommend before the Committee on Rules to institutionalize addressing the prolonged unauthorized absence of members of the Senate,” it added.

At least two senators have been absent from their legislative duties as well as their duties as senator-judges in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte: senators Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa and Loren Legarda.

Dela Rosa has been out of public view due to a pending International Criminal Court warrant of arrest against him while Legarda is under extended medical leave abroad due to a lung illness. – Rappler.com

articles.title: DA to engage in bilateral talks during agri mechanization meet in Manila
articles.summary: The Department of Agriculture (DA) is expected to hold bilateral discussions with representatives from other countries during a global meeting of agricultural leaders and experts in Manila aimed at…

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 5:32pm

The Department of Agriculture (DA) is expected to hold bilateral discussions with representatives from other countries during a global meeting of agricultural leaders and experts in Manila aimed at strengthening agricultural mechanization.
The Philippines is set to host the Asia-Pacific Conference on Sustainable Agricultural Mechanization (APSAM) 2026 on November 23 to 26.
DA spokesperson Arnel de Mesa, however, declined to give further details about the countries that requested to have bilateral talks with the Philippines.

"There will be bilateral discussions. So I cannot divulge at this moment what will be the main agenda for these bilateral discussions. Once we conclude it, we can share it, the results of this bilateral [talks]," he said during the launch of the upcoming summit.
"Again, we received several requests. But I cannot divulge yet the countries," he added.

The conference, organized by the Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations, aims to promote sustainable agricultural mechanization by sharing best practices, and showcasing innovative technologies and financing models.

"It calls for a sustainable agricultural mechanization ecosystem that brings together appropriate technologies, accessible services, financing, policies, and partnerships that respond to the diverse needs of our farmers," said De Mesa.

"By working together, we can accelerate the adoption of appropriate technologies, strengthen agricultural value chains, and build farming systems that are more productive, resilient, and sustainable," he added.
Aside from representatives in Asia Pacific, the conference will also be attended by agricultural representatives from several continents, including Africa. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Teodoro warns: Future generations risk losing WPS resources
articles.summary: OROQUIETA CITY, Misamis Occidental – Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Wednesday warned that future generations of Filipinos could lose access to the country’s maritime resources if the…

blocks.text: OROQUIETA CITY, Misamis Occidental – Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Wednesday warned that future generations of Filipinos could lose access to the country’s maritime resources if the Philippines fails to defend its rights in the West Philippine Sea (WPS).
Teodoro said the country would increasingly need to rely on the sea for resources to sustain its development.

“’Yung mga kailangan natin na resources para mag-asenso, hindi na natin mahahanap sa lupa. Kailangan pumunta tayo sa dagat,” Teodoro said during his remarks at the 97th founding anniversary celebrations in Oroquieta City.
(The resources we need for development can no longer be found on land. We need to turn to the sea.)

“Kaya pinaglalaban natin ang 200 nautical mile exclusive economic zone natin sa West Philippine Sea, sa Pacific Ocean na mas malaki pa, na makuha natin ang fish, ang mga isda, at ang mga oil and gas na nandoon sa ilalim para sa kinabukasan ninyo,” he added.

(That is why we are fighting for our 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone in the West Philippine Sea and the larger area in the Pacific Ocean, so we can benefit from the fish and oil and gas resources there for your future.)
Teodoro warned that others could benefit from these resources if the Philippines failed to protect its maritime rights.
“Kung ubusin namin ’yan, hindi namin labanan ang West Philippine Sea, wala na matitira sa atin. Iba na ang makikinabang,” he said.
(If we exhaust those resources and fail to defend the West Philippine Sea, nothing will be left for us. Others will benefit instead.)
Speaking to reporters afterward, Teodoro described the West Philippine Sea as a key driver of the country’s future development.
“The West Philippine Sea is a catalyst for development,” he said.
“Ngayon, kung we sit back and relax, eh walang mangyayari. Kailangan ipaglaban natin,” he added.
(Now, if we sit back and relax, nothing will happen. We need to fight for it.)
His remarks came amid a renewed dispute with Beijing over joint oil and gas exploration in the West Philippine Sea.

On Tuesday, Teodoro rejected the Chinese Embassy’s accusation that he had obstructed joint exploration efforts, pointing out that former President Rodrigo Duterte terminated negotiations in 2022 over constitutional concerns.
The Philippines and China signed a memorandum of understanding on possible oil and gas cooperation in 2018, but talks ended without a final agreement.

Teodoro also reiterated Wednesday that joint exploration with China would be illegal, citing constitutional concerns and the 2016 arbitral ruling, which invalidated the legal basis of Beijing’s sweeping claims to historic rights in the South China Sea.
China continues to reject the ruling. /jpv

blocks.text: SINGAPORE AIRLINES. A Singapore Airlines Airbus A330-300 plane takes off behind a Boeing 787-10 Dreamliner at Changi Airport in Singapore March 28, 2018.
Edgar Su/Reuters
Singapore Airlines joins Cathay Pacific Airways, Japan Airlines, South Korea's Asiana Airlines, and others that have reported customer data ​was compromised in the Amadeus breach

SINGAPORE – Singapore Airlines said on Tuesday, November 3, that about 46,000 booking records may have been ​affected by a cybersecurity incident involving Amadeus, its reservation technology provider.

The airline joins Cathay Pacific Airways, Japan Airlines, South Korea’s Asiana Airlines, and others that have reported customer data ​was compromised in the Amadeus breach. Malaysia Airlines also said some of its customer information may have been affected
Singapore’s flag carrier said that data exposed by the breach included customers’ names, booking reference numbers, travel itineraries and booking classes
Information including email addresses, phone numbers, travel document details, and KrisFlyer membership numbers may also have been accessed for about 620 booking records, the company said
It added that Amadeus confirmed that bank account or credit card information had not been leaked and bookings were not modified
Singapore Airlines said it was reaching out to affected customers with upcoming travel plans to change their booking reference numbers as a precaution
The airline also confirmed that its IT systems were not breached.
Amadeus ⁠said it had become aware of a vulnerability affecting a travel ​booking display environment but did not ​respond ⁠to a question on how many customers’ data were affected
In recent days, Cathay Pacific and Japan ⁠Airlines ​reported that the breach ​had affected data involving 53,000 bookings and 92,000 customers, respectively – Rappler.com

articles.title: Supreme Court junks Romualdez challenge vs Ombudsman plunder case
articles.summary: The SC en banc rules that the petition has become moot since there's already a plunder case against Romualdez pending before the Sandiganbayan

blocks.text: ARRAIGNED. Former House speaker Martin Romualdez pleads not guilty during his arraignment for plunder, at the New Quezon City Jail on September 16, 2026.
Aaron Favila/AP/Sandiganbayan pool
The SC en banc rules that the petition has become moot since there's already a plunder case against Romualdez pending before the Sandiganbayan

MANILA, Philippines – The Supreme Court (SC) cleared the way for former House speaker Martin Romualdez’s plunder case after it denied the lawmaker’s petition against the Office of the Ombudsman’s investigation.

On Wednesday, November 4, the SC said its en banc denied Romualdez’s certiorari petition against the Ombudsman’s preliminary investigation into his plunder case. The petition also covers the investigative body’s application for a preliminary hold departure order, freeze order, and the alleged use of inadmissible evidence.
Certiorari is a legal remedy that seeks to review another body’s decision for grave abuse of discretion. If granted, it can overturn an order or resolution.

Preliminary investigation is the stage where prosecutors – in this case, the Ombudsman – assess evidence and decide whether to file a case before a court or not. It is the stage before the actual filing of a case.

Meanwhile, the SC also denied Romualdez’s request for a temporary restraining order and/or writ of preliminary injunction to stop the Ombudsman from conducting its preliminary investigation against him.

“The SC ruled that the petition has become moot, or no longer needs to be resolved, because a plunder charge had already been filed against Romualdez before the Sandiganbayan, where he was arraigned and pleaded not guilty. The SC also found no exceptional circumstances that would justify resolving the petition despite its having become moot,” the High Court explained.
Romualdez is facing a corruption case due to alleged P7.44-billion in kickbacks from government projects.

“By repeatedly receiving, directly or indirectly, on at least fifteen (15) occasions, commissions, shares, percentages. kickbacks, ‘commitments’ and/or other pecuniary benefits aggregating at least PhP7,440,000,000.00, by reason or on account of the respective public offices and positions of Romualdez and Co. including monies derived from contractors, persons and entities with interests in flood control, infrastructure and/or other government projects funded under the General Appropriations Acts for fiscal years 2022 to 2025,” the Ombdusman said in the charge.

Romualdez’s petition is indeed moot because the Ombudsman already finished its investigation and filed the plunder case against him with the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan on September 7. On the same day, the anti-graft court’s 3rd Division issued a warrant against Romualdez and ordered his detention.
The lawmaker, who is a first cousin of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., has been detained in New Quezon City Jail in Payatas since September 14.
Plunder is non-bailable so the only way for Romualdez to avail himself of temporary liberty is through a bail petition, which he filed on September 28.
The Sandiganbayan will assess the prosecution’s evidence and if it finds that the evidence of guilt is strong, it might deny Romualdez’s request. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Senate impeachment court asks SC to dismiss Go, Padilla voting threshold petition
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court, through the Office of the Solicitor General, has asked the Supreme Court to dismiss a petition filed by Senators Robin Padilla and Bong Go seeking to declare null the…

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 5:09pm

The Senate impeachment court, through the Office of the Solicitor General, has asked the Supreme Court to dismiss a petition filed by Senators Robin Padilla and Bong Go seeking to declare null the ruling on the voting threshold for Vice President Sara Duterte’s conviction.

“It is respectfully prayed of the Honorable Court to dismiss the Petition for Certiorari and Prohibition for being premature and for lack of merit, and to deny petitioners' application for the issuance of a Status Quo Ante Order, Temporary Restraining Order, and Writ of Preliminary Injunction,” read the 47-page comment filed by the OSG.

In a petition for certiorari and prohibition filed in October, Padilla, Go, and the Partido Demokratiko Pilipino-Lakas ng Bayan (PDP-Laban) asked the SC to issue a status quo ante order or a temporary restraining order directing the Impeachment court and the House of Representatives to refrain from excluding any senator from the count of “all members of the Senate” under the Constitution.
The impeachment court earlier voted to base the “two-thirds of votes” on the number of senators who are capable of "legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings."
Under the 1987 Constitution, no person shall be convicted in an impeachment trial without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the members of the Senate.

The OSG said the authority and responsibility to decide on the voting threshold belongs to the Senate impeachment court, adding that "no grave abuse of discretion can be imputed on the challenged ruling."

It added that the court heard both the defense and prosecution and even invited amici curiae before deciding on the matter. It also noted that the senator-judges deliberated in open session where objections were raised.

"Indisputably, the challenged ruling was a product of a deliberative process where all the parties were given the opportunity to defend their respective positions. Each objection was entertained and resolved," it said.
It further said that the Senate, in ruling on the voting threshold, did not amend but merely interpreted the constitutional provision.

"The Senate's threshold ruling was not an attempt to remove the two-thirds requirement. It was a rule on who should be counted as part of the Senate impeachment court when some senators are unable to take their oaths or participate. Without such a rule, non-participating senators would be counted as though they had performed functions and as if they had voted for acquittal," the OSG said. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Not been this excited in a long time’: US expats ride the blue wave at Australian midterms watch parties
articles.summary:
US voters, their Australian partners and British spectators crowd around pub TVs to watch the historic election results roll in

On the second floor of a Sydney pub, the mood shifts from…

blocks.text: On the second floor of a Sydney pub, the mood shifts from nervous, browser-refreshing anxiety to champagne-popping within a matter of hours.
More than 100 US expats and election enthusiasts pack into the function space at the Keg and Brew in the inner-east suburb of Surry Hills to watch the midterm results roll in.
They’ve followed a sign reading “Democrats Abroad” guiding them upstairs on Wednesday lunch time when live reports began broadcasting on the pub television screens.
Early on, American voters, their Australian partners and British spectators said they were “cautiously optimistic”.
Within a couple of hours in, news of the Democrats’ historic win dramatically shifts the mood.
Katrena Henderson, from North Carolina, says she has “not been this excited about an election in a long time”.
Sitting with her Australian husband and adult son, the trio chronically refresh their phones for results and celebrate when her Senate seat flips to the Democrats.

blocks.caption: Katrena Henderson, a North Carolina voter, says the significance of this election has prompted her to make a political donation for the first time. Photograph: The Guardian

blocks.text: “Nobody, I think, really believed that Democrats were going to do it. And they won decisively,” she says. “It just really points to the fact that Americans want something very different, because this administration is not working for us.
“I think what we didn’t have before today was a lot of hope … and at least now there is some hope.”

Associate Professor David Smith at the University of Sydney’s United States Studies Centre, says the midterms are a “referendum on Trump”. He says the writing was on the wall as voters went to the polls with the president’s approval ratings at a “historically low” level.
“All year, I think Americans have been frustrated by Trump’s lack of focus on things that matter to most Americans,” he says.

“Whether that’s the war in Iran, which most Americans didn’t want and which have sent prices up in a pretty direct way, or whether it’s Trump’s constant beautification projects in Washington, D.C. … All of this is just evidence to a lot of Americans that he is focused on the wrong things and he’s focused on his own self-aggrandisement rather than the country.”

Cindy Herman-Jones moved to Australia from Texas almost 15 years ago and has never cast a vote while living abroad. She says she was compelled to mail in a ballot because of “the stakes of this election” were too high.

“Democracy itself is being attacked by the Trump regime,,” she says. “I just feel like they’ve done so many terrible things, and if he’s in power for another two years with no check on that, then it’s just going to continue to get worse and worse.”

In a list of the “many terrible things” Trump has done, Herman-Jones points to the increased “brutality” of ICE immigration enforcement and the US war in Iran – which she calls “the worst thing” he’s done.
Her vote towards Senator James Talarico saw him flip the Upper house seat, and “amazed” to see him win because “it’s such a hard job for a Democrat to win in Texas”.
Aliana Hensel is another first-time voter. The 18-year-old Californian has lived in Australia for about eight years with her American parents.
She says that while her parents “don’t generally vote” and have not voted while abroad, it was something she wanted to do because “something really, really needs to be done” about US leadership.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Aliana Hensel, 18, voted for the first time in the US midterms. Photograph: The Guardian

blocks.text: “I’ve been watching politics closely for the last few years. It’s something I feel really passionate about. I wasn’t old enough to vote in the presidential election, but I watched that, and it was quite the disappointment,” she says. “So I’ve been very focused on knowing that I can vote this time and wanting to make a bit of an impact.”

Just a couple of kilometres to the north of the Keg and Brew, a small group of election watchers gathered at the Cheers pub off Sydney’s George Street in the CBD over schnitzels and pints of Guinness.
The event was posted as a meetup for some Republican expat groups, but attracted more of a mixed bag of libertarians and independents interested in the drama of an American election.

“It’s interesting to me to see how the populations in America are responding to their situation,” Rahn Wood, 60, an Australian who splits his time between Sydney and Vietnam, said. When asked if he thought Australia and other nations looked towards America when it came to political decisions, Wood said Trump’s influence had a long reach.

blocks.caption: Australian Rahn Wood, 60, at a US midterms election watch event at the Cheers pub in Sydney CBD. Photograph: The Guardian

blocks.text: “I think in a policy sense it does,” he said. “You see that with the green agenda and the support of the United Nations, both of those things are waning because the US – whether it’s Donald Trump or the Congress itself – isn’t very supportive of some of those agendas.

“I think that gives permission, structure for other people to say actually it’s not working for us either,” he went on. “This election helps to set that agenda from a policy point of view does really set the direction for western countries I think.”
Wood added he doesn’t think Australians are interested in anybody as mercurial as Trump, “but, by the same token there’s obviously a big chunk of people that are looking for change”
Others were not optimistic about the results handed down on Fox News, with one woman saying she was watching a growing blue wave with dread. Many had wandered off after lunch.

Professor Smith says while the election “could have significant ramifications as far as things like the Iran war go”, he doubts it will directly influence Australia or Albanese’s relationship to the US because “congress, at the moment, doesn’t have a very big role in foreign policy”.
Smith believes the most interesting is what happens to “Trumpism”.

“There are lots of politicians around the world who take their cues from Trump, including in Australia … If this is an election that really shows the limits of Trumpism in the United States, that could potentially make a few rightwing politicians worldwide rethink how much they want to be tied to Trump,” he says.

articles.title: The give and take (and partisan wrangling) in Alberta's urban-rural hybrid riding maps
articles.summary: The last boundary panel's chair urged the new panel not to alter ridings in southern Alberta. They did.

image.caption: Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi flips through the new report of Alberta's electoral boundaries independent advisory panel at a news conference. (CBC)

blocks.text: When the judge who led Alberta’s boundaries commission gave politicians a narrow path to revise his panel’s work and rescue two rural ridings from the chopping block, Justice Dallas Miller added a few provisos to protect his electoral map work.

The first condition, which the Smith government adopted, stated that “restoration of the two electoral divisions should: have no impact on any electoral division in Airdrie or containing territory south of Airdrie’s southernmost border…”
And lo and behold, where has the new boundary panel done its most controversial redrawing?
In Lethbridge, Calgary and Canmore. All south of Airdrie.
NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi has called it a “Trump-style, MAGA gerrymandered map” that safeguards UCP-held territory in southern Alberta. Adopt it, Nenshi has warned, and “we’ll see them in court.”
Premier Danielle Smith has expressed early favour for the new plan, regardless of its apparent overstepping of the conditions her side set on her new boundary advisory group.

Back in April, when United Conservatives shelved the official commission’s work, she had insisted she was accepting that majority report, just with Justice Dallas Miller’s extra recommendations which proposed modest tweaks.
"You'll see that in his Recommendation Five, he is quite prescriptive about the areas that he thinks are problematic," she told reporters.

The new panel chaired by retired judge Brian O’Ferrall, however, did not feel so fettered about sticking to the confines of what Miller and Alberta’s legislature had set out, stating in its “majority” report that the words in Miller’s fifth recommendation don’t warrant “deification.”
“It was not the ‘Fifth Commandment,’” the report states. “It was simply a bit of political ‘give and take.’”
So what did O’Ferrall’s panel give and take?

It took Lethbridge’s two urban seats and split one of them across three rural ridings that variously stretch up to 150 kilometres in each direction to the U.S. border, the TransCanada Highway, Waterton Lakes National Park and the hamlet of Manyberries, due south of Medicine Hat.
A map showing a sole Lethbridge urban seat, as well as three hybrid electoral divisions combining parts of the city with vast surrounding rural regions. (Advisory panel on electoral boundaries)

It took rural acreage communities from the formerly proposed Cochrane-Springbank riding and dispersed them among three west Calgary districts — which, Nenshi argued, gives thousands of Conservative voters to seats currently held by a trio of UCP cabinet ministers.

It took the Diamond Valley and Longview areas away from adjoining rural ridings south of Calgary and gave them to the Canmore-Banff riding on the other side of Kananaskis Country and a highway partially closed for six months every year.

Not only had Miller, the original commission’s chair, recommended against such tinkering in service of restoring a pair of rural ridings in northern and central Alberta; it’s also not clear that these southern Alberta modifications were even necessary to accommodate the un-eliminating of those two districts.
They weren’t knock-on effects caused by bringing back the riding in Rocky Mountain House and Sundre.
In the case of Springbank and Bearspaw, it was a straightforward bit of subtraction, division and addition, separate from any map work to the north.

According to population figures in the new report, Cochrane’s riding shed 9,703 people, and that same amount was split among the three Calgary ridings, without any corresponding adjustments to any other Calgary constituencies.

It leaves the redesigned Cochrane with 46,785 residents, and 13 per cent below the provincial average riding population. The redrawn Calgary-West-Springbank and Calgary-Bow-Springbank each have more than 58,000 people, nine per cent higher than average.

“Adding Springbank to Calgary Bow is said to potentially favour the party in power,” O’Ferrall’s report acknowledged. “But whether that potential will manifest itself in the next election, not even the pollsters with their voter transpositioning software know for sure.”
Springbank was moved because O’Ferrall and the panel’s UCP appointees felt that rural area had more connection to Calgary than to the small town of Cochrane to its north.

Similarly, it felt that “Lethbridge is not an isolated urban municipality,” but is the hub of southern Alberta’s agri-business, health and service district. Therefore, it partially becomes three hub-and-spoke ridings that nearly stretch from Saskatchewan to British Columbia — and, the NDP argues, erases one of Lethbridge’s politically competitive ridings and dilutes those votes in UCP-friendly zones.
LISTEN | Alberta @ Noon on the boundary revisions:
Alberta at Noon52:39Redrawing Alberta's electoral boundaries
O’Farrell and his UCP-appointed majority dismiss complaints their work is unconstitutional as “polarizing nonsense.”

They take similar umbrage in their report with the NDP-appointed minority’s protests about the new map work in southern Alberta, saying “it can be summarized quite simply. Our proposals are constitutional; yours are not. Our proposals are non-partisan; yours are not.”

For the record, Smith’s cabinet chose O’Ferrall, a former Court of Appeal judge who has donated thousands of dollars to the UCP and federal conservatives since he retired in 2022, and served in court as lawyer for an Alberta Progressive Conservative riding association two decades ago before he was a judge.

The United Conservatives’ two appointees to the panel are Monte Solberg, a former Conservative MP and head of a Calgary-based lobby firm who has donated $2,883 to Smith’s party this year, including some while serving on the panel; and Darwin Durnie, a longtime conservative political donor and municipal public works official who has a lengthy history as a boundary-making hobbyist of sorts, having submitted maps to Alberta’s boundary commissions that propose several rural-urban hybrid ridings.

The NDP’s appointees, constitutional law professor Gerard Kennedy and former Okotoks councillor Brent Robinson, have no record of provincial donations in Elections Alberta’s database. Kennedy has donated federally, predominantly to Conservatives and some to Liberals.
Regardless of how partisan the boundary panelists are or aren’t, the partisan MLAs are set to debate the contentious report in coming days.
Smith likes the idea of Lethbridge’s hybrid ridings, similar to how Medicine Hat is divided between her Brooks-Medicine Hat seat and a UCP colleague’s Cypress-Medicine Hat.

“I represent a hybrid riding, and I think Medicine Hat is well-served by having two representatives. I think Lethbridge will be very well-served by having four representatives,” she told reporters Tuesday.

Premier Danielle Smith, who represents a rural-urban hybrid riding in Medicine Hat, said Lethbridge would be well-served by having several rural-urban hybrid MLAs instead of two city-only MLAs. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

The NDP cannot launch a lawsuit against this new riding map until the legislature approves it and puts it into effect. A successful challenge would have to argue that the ridings violate the “effective representation” guarantees in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms — such a claim could theoretically come from a political party, or the affected residents in Lethbridge or elsewhere, including the few thousand people in Springbank and Bearspaw who find themselves mixed into 50,000-person-plus seats in Alberta’s biggest city.

Original commission chair Miller, for his part, wrote in his report that he didn’t find Lethbridge or Springbank hybrids “necessarily unreasonable or procedurally unfair,” noting that some public members proposed them to the commission. But that report blurb wasn’t part of the government motion that created the do-over boundary review, unlike the one urging against any redrawing work south of Airdrie.

Smith discussed on Tuesday being ready to “assemble a legal team” ahead of a potential court challenge. When asked about Miller’s warning on southern ridings she said: “I'll take a closer look at it and talk to the lawyers about that.”

articles.title: A runner died in the New York City Marathon. Have the risks changed as more people race?
articles.summary: Every year, amid our current running boom, more and more people vie for the chance to lace up their sneakers and push themselves 42.2 kilometres to cross that finish line. But every year, young and…

image.caption: Runners cross the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge during the New York City Marathon on Sunday. Rachel Apa died only a few kilometres from the finish. (Heather Khalifa/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Every year, amid our current running boom, more and more people vie for the chance to lace up their sneakers and push themselves 42.2 kilometres to cross that finish line. But every year, young and seemingly healthy people also die trying.
Rachel Apa, 24, died after collapsing just over 3 km from the finish line
She was just a few kilometres from the finish line.
A record-breaking 61,146 runners completed the New York City Marathon on Sunday. But Rachel Apa, despite being in what her father describes as perfect health, wasn't one of them.

The 24-year-old athlete collapsed near mile 24, or about 38.6 kilometres into the 42.2-kilometre race. Despite the life-saving efforts of bystanders, paramedics and then hospital doctors, she was pronounced dead later that night, her grieving parents told the New York Times.
"It's unfathomable," her father Steve Apa, who could not be reached by CBC News, told the news outlet.

Every year, more and more people vie for the chance to lace up their sneakers and push themselves 42.2 kilometres to cross that finish line. But every year, young and seemingly healthy people also die trying — typically of heart failure or cardiac arrest.

All told, including Rachel Apa, at least six runners have died racing in marathons and half-marathons around the world in the past six months alone. Still, experts say the incidence rate is very low, given that millions of people run them every year.

Marathons aren't any riskier than they were 20 years ago, but they are far more popular, explained Jack Goodman, a professor emeritus in kinesiology at the University of Toronto, and adjunct scientist of cardiovascular research at Toronto's University Health Network.
"When the population is so large, there are bound to be more cases, rare as they are," Goodman told CBC News.

Any time you have thousands of people in the same space, based on probabilities, one of them will have a cardiac event, Dr. Christopher Labos, a cardiologist and epidemiologist in Montreal, told CBC News.
"You just hear about it more in the news because it's so shocking when something unexpected like this happens."
Rachel Apa is pictured in the 2023 field hockey roster on the athletics website for Bucknell University in Lewisburg, Pa. (Bucknellbison.com)
Risk of dying has decreased: study

Anyone who has tried to register for a marathon in the last few years can tell you how popular they've become. A record 1.3 million people have already applied to run the 2027 London Marathon. So many people have tried to register for the Boston Marathon in recent years that they've tightened their qualifying times.

In the U.S. alone, more than 29 million people completed marathons and half-marathons in between 2010 and 2023, notes a 2025 study published the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA). That's triple the number compared to a decade earlier, the authors add.

items: 70-year-old Ottawa woman sets new marathon world record
More kids are running marathons. A teen's death reignites a debate about the risks

blocks.text: Overall, the risk of risk of death is about one in 150,000 runners, notes a 2019 global review in the BMJ medical journal. Typically, the risk is much higher for men, the cause is often coronary artery disease and the deaths most often occur in the last quarter of the race, the study says.
"There are infrequent deaths, which are often reported widely, and may create unnecessary alarm about the potential risks," the authors wrote.

The 2025 JAMA study points out that the risk of dying from a cardiac event during long-distance running races in the U.S. has actually gone down by about 50 per cent in recent years — likely due to more effective emergency planning, including access to defibrillators.

But the study also noted a small uptick in non-fatal cardiac events since 2020, which the authors hypothesized could be due to less access to health care during the COVID-19 pandemic, leading to reduced detection of cardiovascular disease.
Runners make their way through Queens during the New York City Marathon Sunday. (Heather Khalifa/The Associated Press)
Usually a pre-existing cause, expert says
Most often, in the case of death, there's underlying coronary disease the runner didn't know about and never caused them a problem until the race, said Goodman.
"Sudden cardiac death is, unfortunately, not a terribly uncommon first symptom of heart disease," he said.

Just last month, 24-year-old Treyton Lara collapsed at mile 20 of the Portland Marathon and died. He'd experienced a sudden cardiac arrest, his family said. In January, Julien Autissier, 33, collapsed around the 19-mile mark of the Miami marathon and died in the hospital. Doctors also suspected sudden cardiac arrest, according to the Miami New Times.

Roland Liinar, 25, died last May after collapsing in the Rimi Riga Marathon in Latvia. The same month, two other runners died after collapsing while competing in half-marathons in New York and the U.K.

Still, from a public health perspective, the problem most people have is moving too little, not moving too much, said Lagos, the cardiologist and epidemiologist. And if you're a young healthy person who trained properly for a marathon, a cardiac event is "almost certainly not going to happen in your case."
Runners cross the finish line in Central Park on Sunday. (Angelina Katsanis/The Associated Press)
'She did everything she's supposed to'

Apa, an industrial-technology product manager, had run to raise money for Parkinson's disease in honour of her grandfather. On her fundraiser page, which had raised more than $26,000 US by Tuesday evening, Apa called him her "role model."

New York Road Runners, the non-profit club that stages the New York City Marathon, said in a news release that CPR was administered to Apa by a bystander and later by event medical staff. A defibrillator was also used before paramedics took Apa to the Mount Sinai Hospital, reports The Associated Press.
The former Division I field hockey player at Bucknell University was in critical condition when she was brought to the hospital, where doctors unsuccessfully tried to save her for several hours.

items: A workout class sent this St. John's woman to hospital. She's not the only one
'Extreme' workouts drive spike in 'rhabdo' cases among young N.L. women, says doctor

blocks.text: Steve Apa says Rachel's cause of death Sunday was rhabdomyolysis, a rare but serious condition where the muscle cells break down and leak into the bloodstream. Rhabdo, as it is often called, can be brought on by severe physical exertion.

Exercise-induced rhabdo cases aren't tracked across Canada, CBC News has previously reported. But there was recently a spike of cases in young women in St. John's, with health officials pointing to intense workouts and social media competitiveness.
It was her first marathon, but Rachel was a lifelong athlete, her father told USA Today, and she had trained carefully for months.
"She did everything she's supposed to."
Dangerous fitness: What is rhabdomyolysis?

blocks.text: Politics·New

Canada wants to split its planned purchase of 12 German submarines, committing to eight up front while leaving the remaining four for a future decision. Sources tell CBC News the proposal is intended to preserve financial flexibility but could jeopardize some of the $86 billion in economic benefits promised by Germany.
Proposal to batch order of up to 12 subs raises questions about economic benefits
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 04, 2026 4:00 AM EST | Last Updated: 30 minutes ago

Canadian negotiators have proposed to break up the purchase of Type 212CD submarines from Germany into two batches with a guaranteed upfront buy of eight boats and a proposal to acquire another four in the future, CBC News has learned.

The proposal was made during a series of meetings that took place last week in Ottawa between federal officials — led by the Defence Investment Agency — and representatives of German submarine-maker TKMS and Norwegian defence giant Kongsberg.
Three confidential sources tell CBC News that the Canadian side has been talking for several weeks — since a round of meetings in Europe in September — about breaking up the order.
German government officials have been studying what impact a reduced order might have on the $86 billion in economic investment in Canada that was promised last summer.
Carney chooses German submarines for Canadian navy fleet
At the same time, TKMS is talking with its 400 suppliers about how a potentially smaller order would affect them.

When Prime Minister Mark Carney announced last July that his government had chosen the TKMS proposal over rival Hanwha Ocean of South Korea, he made clear that Canada was committed to buying "up to 12 submarines."

The confidential sources say, since the delivery of the boats won't start until the mid-2030s — and will likely carry on for more than a dozen years afterward — the sense among federal officials is that they want to preserve the flexibility of future governments to make decisions.
The sources also say there's a debate about whether crewed submarines will eventually be replaced by more effective or cheaper drone technology.

The purchase of 12 new submarines to replace the navy's aging Victoria-Class boats is estimated to cost between $20 billion and $24 billion. The full cycle cost — from operations, maintenance and repairs — is expected to run over $100 billion over two decades.
One of the confidential sources said the Canadian side has also indicated that cost is a consideration.

items: Why is Canada spending tens of billions on new submarines?

blocks.text: The navy has set the requirement at 12 boats based on the anticipation it will be asked to patrol the country's three-ocean coastline and participate in allied missions overseas, notably in the Indo-Pacific.

A spokesperson for Stephen Fuhr, the secretary of state for defence procurement, said the federal government reiterated that the prime minister's pledge was for "up to 12 modern submarines that will help to protect Canadians by replacing the aging Victoria-Class fleet."

Sofiya Sapeha said the Defence Investment Agency is continuing negotiations with the preferred supplier "and is working to secure a contract that ensures maximum benefits for Canadians across the country."
Sapeha added: "Because the procurement process is currently active, we are unable to comment on the content and status of the negotiations."
8 subs still 'a very large number'
Carney set a deadline of achieving a contract by no later than the end of 2027.

One source with knowledge of the proposal said the federal government has been consistent in its language in the run-up to the decision — and throughout negotiations — that it was interested in "up to 12" boats and that an upfront commitment of eight was still "a very large number" of submarines.
A spokesperson for TKMS said negotiations with the Canadian government remain on track, but declined to get into specifics.
"The Canadian Patrol Submarine Project aims to acquire 12 submarines that will help to protect Canadians by replacing the aging Victoria-Class fleet," said Andrew Bernardo.

"TKMS is working diligently with the government of Canada to finalize an agreement. As partners, we remain fully engaged in the process. With negotiations ongoing, it would be premature to comment on their details or potential outcomes."
Bernardo added that "negotiations continue productively, and we are focused on advancing the long-term strategic partnership in a manner that maximizes opportunities for Canadian industry."
Last week, the head of the German Parliament's defence committee, Thomas Röwekamp, was also in Ottawa.
Who is accountable for new defence Crown corp?

He was not part of the negotiations, but said he was aware of the proposal. He said he was confident that Canada, Germany and Norway, which is also a partner in the deal, would hammer out their differences.
"We are working on that and it is a government-to-government relationship in which we discussed so many details of this deal," Röwekamp said.
"This is not only a deal between a German company and the Canadian government. It is also a part of strategic partnership as well."
Röwekamp said the deal is also important for NATO.

"We hope they will order 12, and we are doing a lot to make the deal real," Röwekamp said, pointing to the decision by both Germany and Norway to give up production slots in order for Canada to receive four boats by 2036. "So yes, we are very interested in having the deal in total."
Since Canadian shipyards don't currently have the capacity to build submarines, the federal government sought proposals from both bidders for economic benefits.

The Germans said they were prepared to partner with Alberta to construct a large-scale carbon capture facility utilizing proprietary TKMS industrial technology. There was also a plan to invest directly in the modernization and expansion of the Port of Churchill in Manitoba in order to export liquefied natural gas (LNG) and critical minerals.

items: Billions more for defence, but Canada's military still faces an old budget squeeze
Norway PM 'prepared, but not afraid' of Russian incursion

blocks.text: The German pitch also called for the building of a factory to manufacture heavy torpedoes and to conduct joint development and testing of hypersonic missiles, among other things.
The submarine purchase would also require the construction of dedicated maintenance facilities on both coasts.
Defence analyst Dave Perry said that breaking up the order from TKMS could come with "downsides."
He said the scale of promised economic benefits could be reduced unless "you commit at the beginning to buying the whole enchilada."
Canada could lose sway with suppliers if it reduces sub commitment: defence analyst

Perry also noted that breaking up the order is not unheard of and pointed to the federal government's plans to buy 15 new destroyers for the navy. In that program, the federal government committed to an initial purchase of three warships from Irving Shipbuilding Inc. in Halifax.

"I think the other thing that we've done in the past with other shipbuilding procurement is use a batching strategy as basically a risk mitigation initiative," said Perry, the president of the Canadian Global Affairs Institute.
"You don't commit fully, you commit to a smaller buy, you then revisit the decision and that kind of controls the financial obligation on the part of the government."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.

articles.title: Miliband criticises Blair’s slavery statement and defends Burnham’s plan for proper apology – UK politics live
articles.summary:
The foreign secretary added that the UK will not shift its position on reparations

Good morning. Wednesdays are normally the most exciting day of the week at Westminster, because it’s PMQs,…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 2m agoBurnham says Commonwealth 'more important today than ever before'

blocks.text: Burnham says Commonwealth 'more important today than ever before'

Andy Burnham has described the Commonwealth as “more important today than ever before” amid “such volatile times”. He used the phrase in a meeting with his Antigua and Barbuda counterpart Gaston Browne, who is hosting the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm).
In a readout of the meeting, released this morning, a No 10 spokesperson said:

double quotation markThe prime minister thanked Prime Minister Browne for the warm welcome from Antigua and Barbuda and for hosting Commonwealth leaders at such an important time. In such volatile times, it was clear that the Commonwealth was more important today than ever before, the prime minister added.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham (right) with Gaston Browne  ahead of a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Chogm. Photograph: Kin Cheung/PA

blocks.text: Good morning. Wednesdays are normally the most exciting day of the week at Westminster, because it’s PMQs, but today (unless we get some mega surprise) all the action is taking place somewhere else. In part, that’s because Andy Burnham is still at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua. But mostly because anyone in SW1 with even a passing interest in politics will be far more interested in the outcome of the US midterm elections. You can catch up with all the drama on our US politics live blog.

While the US results are undoubtedly fascinating, quite how relevant they are to the UK is a bit harder to discern. Donald Trump is still president for the next two years, and none of the chaos he has caused for Britain and other European allies is going to go away; conceivably, he could end up even more disruptive. Trump was first elected president in 2016 only months after the UK voted for Brexit and there will be progressives in Britain hoping the US results show that what Ed Davey is this morning calling the “politics of hate, division and economic harm” might be on their way out this side of the pond too. Maybe? But it is probably too soon to get carried away. Our US coverage is all here. In so far as there is any interesting UK reaction, I will post it here.

Back to the Commonwealth summit, and Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has given an interview to the BBC in which he defended Burnham’s decision to open talks about a proper UK apology for slavery. In particular, Miliband was critical of Tony Blair’s attempts to settle this issue with what Miliband described as a “sorry not sorry” apology.

Miliband was referring to this statement that Blair issued in 2006, written up at the time by the Guardian here. Blair said the slave trade was “profoundly shameful” and he expressed “deep sorrow that it ever happened”. But he did not formally apologise.
In an interview with the BBC’s Newscast podcast, Miliband said Burnham wanted a different approach. He said:

double quotation markPeople have been honestly a bit bruised by the past, what happened in the past, the sense that we just really just wanted to sweep this issue under the carpet and not confront it. My sense is there’s a bit of a sigh of relief that, OK … at least there’s a sense of we’ve got a shared interest now in moving the Commonwealth on.
Miliband said Blair “did sort of do a kind of sorry not sorry situation”. He added: “He kind of expressed ‘sorrow, but’ and then said sorry, and then it was walked back by No 10.”

(Miliband has for many years had a strained relationship with the former prime minister, who was opposed to the way Miliband criticised some aspects of New Labour’s record when he was party leader between 2010 and 2015. These latest remarks are just the latest example of feuding between the two of them.)

Burnham has said he wants a “structured dialogue” with Commonwealth countries about the wording of an apology. Asked whether the government might reach the point of a formal apology by the time it hosts the G20 leaders’ summit in Manchester next November, Miliband said: “Broadly speaking, yes.”
But he also stressed that the UK was not offering reparations. Asked whether the government’s new approach could end up costing UK taxpayers a penny more, Miliband replied:

double quotation markNo … For us, that’s never been what it’s about. And that’s why it’s been important that … I did have this conversation with our partners in advance. I said, ‘Look, we are going to say we are willing to say that we’re open to an apology, but we’re not going to shift our position on reparations.’ It’s not for us. It’s not the right answer. It’s not practical. It’s not feasible for us, but there are things we can work on co-operatively.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.30am: Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, gives evidence to the Commons health committee.
10am: Lucy Powell, the education secretary, gives evidence to the Commons education committee.
Noon: Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, faces Alex Burghart, the deputy Conservative leader, at PMQs.
Afternoon (UK time): Andy Burnham is due to record a pooled TV interview while attending the final day of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda.
2.15pm: Jonathan Haskel, chair of the Office for Budget Responsibility, gives evidence with colleagues to the Commons Treasury committee about the budget.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: In new study, think tank raises several red flags over expanded oil exploration in Palawan
articles.summary: Palawan"s marine biodiversity and food system are at risk amid expanded oil exploration around the island, according to a new study published by non-government organization Center for Energy,…

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 4:54pm

Palawan’s marine biodiversity and food system are at risk amid expanded oil exploration around the island, according to a new study published by non-government organization Center for Energy, Ecology, and Development (CEED).

The scoping paper titled “Don’t Drill Paradise,” authored by researcher Charlene Jemima Lopez, analyzed the government’s different national policies and agreements on fuel, and utilized different case studies to show the impacts of oil exploration.

“Despite the province’s ecological and environmental importance, upstream exploration and production activities are concentrated in Palawan. It hosts 14 active offshore petroleum service contracts, with several additional applications pending in nearby areas,” the study found.

CEED raised several risks to the environment when it came to expanded oil exploration, including seismic airguns that caused harmful noise to marine life, as well as the drilling of wells that damage the seabed.
Methane, a principal component of fossil gas and a potent greenhouse gas, contributed significantly to near-total global warming. This methane could escape through equipment leaks, venting, and more.

Coastal communities are also directly impacted by these upstream activities, with fisherfolk reporting lower catches. Every stage of gas projects posed a risk of oil contamination which could devastate the marine ecosystem, leading to fishing bans and the closure of tourism industries.
Government policies also tended to favor large conglomerates, offering little protection for host communities.

“The law provides no clear mechanism for reparations for damages suffered by communities or the environment. It merely requires contractors to give priority in employment to qualified local residents, effectively reducing host communities to a source of labor, while any direct community benefits remain discretionary and dependent on negotiations between the national government and the contractor,” the study read.
The study also raised alarm over the environmental damage to the food system in Palawan.
Since Palawan fisheries are already under pressure from overfishing, upstream oil activities could make it further vulnerable.

“Reduced fish catch would not only undermine the incomes of fishing communities but constrain the availability and affordability of fish as a source of food–resulting in higher prices that could affect the whole country,” the study found.
Based on its findings, the study concluded that the Marcos administration has delayed the country’s transition into using renewable energy,

“The current policy directions of the Marcos administration places communities and marine life at risk while delaying, rather than facilitating, the transition to renewable energy. Gas exploration and production disrupts marine ecosystems even before gas reserves are discovered. At the same time, large investments in the fossil gas industry divert resources away from renewable energy and lock the country into prolonged fossil-fuel dependence,” the study read.

In 2022, Marcos called fossil gas as an interim fuel while the country transitioned into renewable energy. Liquified natural gas (LNG) was also considered a necessary transition fuel under the Philippine Energy Plan.
Despite this, CEED said there was a “gas boom” under the Marcos administration. Before the Marcos admin, there were only 10 petroleum service contracts (PSC).
Twelve new PSC’s were awarded during his term, raising the country’s contracts to 22.

“If gas truly is a ‘transition fuel’, fossil gas should be phased out after displacing coal and oil in the energy mix. Yet, until now, there is no oil and coal phase-out and neither is there any plan to phase out gas after it has supposedly acted as a transition fuel,” the research said.

The Marcos admin has been urged to phase out fossil fuels and to halt the development of gas fields and awarding of PSCs. The study also recommended strengthening environmental and social safeguards for oil and gas activities.
The CEED also urged the local government of Palawan to reject new development of gas projects and to invest in renewable energy solutions.
Stakeholders are also urged to participate in consultations and demand transparency.
GMA News has reached out to the Department of Energy and the Palace for response to these findings. — LA, GMA News

articles.title: SC amends e-rules for child witnesses; allows video conference, recorded interviews
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has approved the use of video conferencing and other means of technology to protect children if they need to recount traumatic experiences.

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 4:47pm
The Supreme Court (SC) has approved the use of video conferencing and other means of technology to protect children if they need to recount traumatic experiences.
In a news release on Wednesday, the SC approved the Revised Rule on the Examination of Child Witnesses (RRECW), which updated how children are questioned in court.

“Key changes include the use of videoconferencing, recorded depositions, recorded interviews, and technological tools to help children explain what happened. These technological tools are in addition to existing testimonial aids such as dolls, drawings, and puppets,” the SC said in a statement.
“Courts may allow children to testify via videoconferencing from outside the courtroom if testifying in person is likely to cause them trauma,” the high court added.
Apart from this, the court may also limit who the child can see and hear, including the accused. However, the accused’s right to confront the witness remains preserved.
Should the child need to identify the accused, the accused may briefly turn on the camera. The child may identify the accused from an image displayed on a screen.

“If a child cannot testify at trial or via videoconferencing due to a disability, health concerns, or other reasons, the child’s testimony may be taken through an electronically recorded deposition in the presence of the judge and lawyers for both sides. The recording may be used in place of the child’s in-court testimony,” the SC said.

Children also cannot be forced to appear and court and must not be present if sexually explicit materials are shown. Records about children are confidential, and anyone found posting them may be held in contempt by the court.
The RRECW also encourages and allows a recorded interview with the child, which will be conducted by a team of professionals.
The recording or the transcript may be presented as evidence, as long as the interviewer asked neutral, open-ended, age-appropriate, and trauma-informed questions without suggesting answers.
The new set of rules applies to children who are victims of crimes, children in conflict with the law, and child witnesses in all cases. —Jean Mangaluz/RF, GMA News

articles.title: [In This Economy] Pax Silica: What’s the Philippines’ trump card?
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump’s visit to the Philippines this month gives President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. a good occasion to explain what we’re negotiating for on Pax Silica

blocks.text: In case you missed it, US President Donald Trump is soon coming to the Philippines. Malacañang has confirmed his attendance at the ASEAN Summit and related meetings in Manila on November 16 to 18.

One deal that Philippine officials had hoped to sign around the time of his visit is the framework for the proposed Pax Silica industrial hub in New Clark City. But as of Tuesday November 3, Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) chief Joshua Bingcang said the framework had been submitted to Malacañang and there was still no signing date. Whether there will be a signing during the visit, and whether Trump himself will sign, remains open.

But in fact, the Philippines already joined Pax Silica in April when it signed the declaration. That brought us into a US-led effort to build more secure supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductors, and other technologies that underpin artificial intelligence. The framework now awaiting signature concerns how the proposed 4,000-acre hub in Tarlac would be developed.
Even after that agreement is signed, we’ll still have to see which companies actually invest, what they build, and what they commit to doing here.
The signing date has gotten a lot of attention. But in this piece, I’d like to explore exactly what the Marcos administration is asking for in return. What’s in it for us?
Two recent papers by my UP School of Economics (UPSE) colleague Annette Balaoing-Pelkmans help explain what’s at stake.
In her paper for the UP Center for Integrative and Development Studies (UP CIDS), she draws a distinction between hosting an industry and acquiring the capabilities to do more valuable work in it.

Take semiconductors. Say a multinational opens a plant in Clark and hires Filipino engineers to run equipment that tests chips. Over time, those engineers get better at their jobs: they can test more chips in a day, catch defects earlier, and waste fewer materials.

All of that is valuable, for sure. But imagine that the Filipino team also gets to develop the tests, figure out why the chips are failing, and work with the design team to fix the problem. That’s a different kind of gain. The engineers can take on more complex work, and those skills can travel to other firms or help start new ones. That would be a genuine technology transfer.

You see, the Philippines already assembles and tests semiconductors. The question is how much more of the engineering we’ll get to do. Any foreign company can set up shop in Tarlac and still have its tests designed abroad, buy most of its sophisticated inputs from its usual suppliers, and keep its research at headquarters. Its factory can create jobs and boost exports while leaving our place in the supply chain largely where it was.

Annette’s other paper, a UPSE Discussion Paper, is written from the perspective of the Tatak Pinoy Strategy, helps explain why that can happen. Drawing on consultations in electronics, semiconductors, and IT and business process management, she points to capabilities we already have in areas like chip design and cybersecurity.

The difficulty, she says, is getting more firms and workers to build on them. Take for instance the case of MYPAD, an effort to strengthen microelectronics education and connect it with industry. It lost momentum for lack of sustained institutional backing.
It takes years to train engineers, develop suppliers, and build research partnerships. The institutions doing that work need funding and a clear mandate well after the launch event is over.
There’s another important question to ask: How much of the investment would have happened anyway?

Suppose a company was already looking to expand its Philippine operations. If the government offers it a tax break to move that expansion to Clark, officials might count the entire factory as a win for Pax Silica.

For taxpayers, the relevant gain is whatever the offer actually secured beyond the company’s original plans. Perhaps the firm adds an engineering team, or gives local suppliers a route to qualify for contracts. We should be able to say what that extra benefit is and how much we paid for it.

The same scrutiny should apply to what we build with public money in support of Pax Silica. A more reliable power grid and better freight links can serve many businesses, whether or not the hub attracts its intended tenants.

Infrastructure built for a single investor is a different proposition. Who pays if that investor backs out? And before committing land and water to a project, what will be left for nearby communities and farms in a dry year? Those questions deserve answers while we still have leverage to change the terms.

As Trump’s arrival approaches, let us demand answers to the following questions: Exactly how many Filipinos will be trained and given responsibility for advanced engineering work? Will local firms get a chance to qualify as suppliers, and who will help them meet the standards? If public money goes into joint research, what rights will Philippine universities and firms have to use the results? And what happens to the incentives if the investor falls short?

blocks.caption: [In This Economy] Risks of Pax Silica

blocks.text: In the end, Trump’s visit gives President Marcos a good occasion to explain what we’re negotiating for. He can start by making the proposed terms public and telling us what Filipinos are being asked to put up for the project.

Perhaps Marcos should take a leaf from Trump’s own book. In The Art of the Deal, Trump and his coauthor Tony Schwartz write, “The worst thing you can possibly do in a deal is seem desperate to make it.”

Honestly, I’m no Trump fan, but that’s actually good advice worth taking. Marcos has no reason to treat Pax Silica as our last chance to upgrade Philippine manufacturing. If the terms still need work when Trump comes to Manila, the deal can wait.

The US wants more secure supply chains, and we can offer a site in Clark and decades of experience in semiconductor assembly and testing. In return, though, Marcos should ask for specific commitments on what engineering work will be done here and how Filipino firms can qualify for supplier contracts.
We have a trump card—and we should use it. – Rappler.com

Jan Carlo “JC” Punongbayan, PhD, is an associate professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics. His professional experience includes the Securities and Exchange Commission, the World Bank Office in Manila, the Far Eastern University Public Policy Center, and the National Economic and Development Authority. JC writes a weekly economics column for Rappler. He is also co-founder of UsapangEcon.com and co-host of Usapang Econ Podcast.

His first book, False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, was published by Ateneo de Manila University Press in February 2023. His second book, Twin Plagues: How Duterte and COVID-19 Wrecked the Philippine Economy, was published by Penguin Random House SEA in June 2026. Follow him on Instagram (@jcpunongbayan).
