NBI Director Melvin Matibag in the witness stand at the impeachment proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte on July 22, 2026.
Senate PRIB
MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is preparing to issue subpoenas as it investigates the alleged dumping of pet remains in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan.
NBI Director Melvin Matibag announced the move during a Tuesday, November 3 meeting with pet owners and representatives of non-government organizations assisting in the investigation.
"We can subpoena the personalities. Yung tao at saka yung dokumento nila. Definitely, dapat may record 'yan," Matibag said.
(We can subpoena the people involved and their documents. Definitely, there should be records.)
Matibag said investigators were looking into possible estafa and violations of environmental laws, among other liabilities, over the alleged improper disposal of animal remains.
He also described the alleged conduct as a betrayal of public trust.
Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) Executive Director Anna Cabrera, meanwhile, said the organization had gathered 191 affidavits and submissions from pet owners.
Of these, 25 pet owners had retrieved their pets' remains, while 12 had formally sought PAWS' assistance.
The investigation began after the remains of 26 dogs and three cats were found in plastic bags along a roadside in San Jose del Monte City.
Following the discovery, the Bacoor City government ordered the closure of Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium.
Bacoor Mayor Strike Revilla also directed the Philippine National Police to investigate the establishment's owner and pursue appropriate charges.

articles.title: Anthony Zurcher: Democrats eye sweeping gains and reshaping of political map
articles.summary: Two Senate races that a year ago were thought to be battlegrounds turned out to be slam-dunks for the Democrats.

blocks.text: This is already shaping up to be a very good night for Democrats, with much of the vote counted in the eastern United States and polls closing in key Midwestern battleground states.

Two Senate races that a year ago were thought to be battlegrounds have turned out to be slam dunks for the Democrats - Jon Ossoff's re-election race in Georgia and the open Republican-held seat in North Carolina.

That North Carolina contest, where former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper bested Republican Party insider Michael Whatley, was the first of the four pick-ups Democrats need in order to wrest control of the Senate.
Attention has now turned to Republican-held Senate seats in Texas, Kansas and Ohio, where counting is taking place.
In South Carolina, the BBC's US partner CBS News is rating the Senate race as leaning Democrat, which would be an earth-shaking result.
If you look at key races in House of Representatives, there are other encouraging signs for Democrats.
In Florida, Republicans in the state legislature had redrawn the boundaries of three Democratic-held seats to make it much easier to for them to win.
They lost all three.

items: US midterm elections results 2026
Live updates

blocks.text: Other House races in the state, where Republicans expected to win by comfortable margins, have turned out to be dogfights.
Democrats flipped an open seat in western North Carolina, for instance, and appear in position to make gains in Virginia, Kentucky and Indiana.
In races considered toss-ups across the east, Democrats are poised for the kind of victories that will help secure a House majority for the first time since 2022.
They're doing it on the back of high Democratic turnout, particularly by black voters in the south, and winning back Hispanic voters in Florida who had supported the Republicans just two years ago.
In majority black South Carolina counties, Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews is significantly outperforming Kamala Harris's presidential numbers in 2024.
And in Miami-Dade County, which Trump carried that year, Democratic candidates are back on top.

articles.title: Killer who escaped Tennessee prison captured after week-long manhunt
articles.summary: Jacob Allen Morley was serving a life sentence for murder before he escaped over a prison fence.

blocks.text: US authorities have recaptured a convicted murderer who escaped a Tennessee prison more than a week ago.

Jacob Allen Morley, 28, was serving a life sentence over the killing of his colleague in 2022, when he escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, about 90 miles (145 km) north of Memphis.

The Tennessee Department of Correction (TDOC) said security footage showed Morley, wearing his prison uniform, breaching the prison fence around 11:30pm on 25 October, and later stealing a vehicle from a nearby farm.
On Wednesday the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI) announced Morley was in custody after an operation that involved local, state and federal agencies.
In a statement, the TBI said authorities had received a tip that Morley was hiding on an Illinois property, from which a truck had also been stolen.
The truck's licence plate was then tracked through automatic plate-reader technology, travelling through Missouri, where local authorities were dispatched to follow.

Morley was apprehended by Missouri State Highway Patrol "without incident" in Carroll County at 11:34am local time on Tuesday. Three firearms that had previously been reported stolen were also recovered from the vehicle, the TBI said.
Photos published by authorities showed Morley handcuffed and being led out of a field by officers.
Morley was convicted of first-degree murder over the death of his colleague Cody Birchfield in 2022. He was sentenced in June 2025. His request for a new trial was denied in May.
Birchfield's body was found in a metal box under Morley's home, according to Carter County court records reviewed by the BBC.
Birchfield died "as a result of a gunshot wound to the back of the head", a pathology report cited in court said. Bullet casings matched a gun found in Morley's house.

Birchfield's sister said in her victim impact statement to the court that the pair had developed a friendship while Birchfield was training Morley at the pallet manufacturing company where they were both employed.
Besides murder, Morley was also convicted of vandalism, tampering with evidence, aggravated burglary, and evading arrest.
This is not the first time Morley has led law enforcement officials on a manhunt. His 2022 arrest came after a police chase that crossed state lines into North Carolina.
The Northwest Correctional Complex is a men's prison with the capacity to hold up to 1,776 inmates, from low security to maximum, the BBC's partner CBS reported.
CBS said the prison has seen numerous acts of violence in recent years, and in July a grand jury returned dozens of indictments over assaults on staff and the murders of five inmates.

articles.title: 2024 heatwave linked to 585 more preterm births in Philippines — study
articles.summary: Extreme heat in April 2024 resulted in 585 additional preterm births during the 15-day period, where temperatures rose 2.44 degrees above normal.

blocks.text: Climate and Environment
November 4, 2026 | 10:07am
A mother holds her baby born in a leap year at a maternity hospital in Manila on February 29, 2024.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — Nearly 600 more babies were born too early in the Philippines during the April 2024 heatwave, a new study estimates, as the country heads into another stretch of extreme heat under a strong El Niño.

Zero Carbon Analytics, an international think tank on climate change and the energy transition, estimates an additional 585 babies were born preterm during the 15-day extreme heat event, a 10% increase above average April figures.
The World Health Organization defines "preterm births" as those occurring before 37 weeks.

Temperatures during the 15-day spell ran 2.44 degrees Celsius above normal. At its peak, the town of Iba, Zambales logged a heat index of 53 degrees Celsius, one of the highest readings of the year at the time.

Climate change, according to the organization, caused the pre-monsoon weather to be 1.2 degrees hotter, leading to a separate estimate of 263 preterm births that would not have occurred without human-caused warming.

Zero Carbon Analytics compared the Philippines' statistics for April 2024 to the country's average April based on data from 1991 to 2020, following a baseline established by the World Meteorological Organization. Results were reported at a 95% confidence level.
Calabarzon saw the highest nominal increase at 100 births, closely followed by Metro Manila and Central Luzon with around 80 births each.
Cagayan Valley, however, had the highest rise in risk: Cagayan province experienced temperatures 4.01 degrees hotter than normal, resulting in a 17% surge.

Babies born too early are more prone to breathing problems, infections, difficulty feeding and trouble keeping warm, according to the World Health Organization. Complications of preterm birth are the leading cause of death among children under five worldwide, and many survivors live with lifelong disabilities, including learning difficulties and problems with sight and hearing.
A nation at risk
The Philippines was ranked seventh in Germanwatch's Climate Risk Index, meaning that heat-specific exposure is rising faster in the country than in most parts of the world.

Between 2020 and 2024, the country experienced 36 days with maximum temperatures above a threshold linked to increased preterm birth risk. Climate change is thought to be responsible for 30 of these days, given that a 1-degree increase in temperature is associated with 4% higher odds of preterm birth.
Women and newborns living in poverty are especially vulnerable due to limited access to healthcare, mobility, and resources to support traditional livelihoods.

The Climate Change Commission warned that temperatures could reach 45 to 50 degrees in treeless urban areas during Super El Niño, which began in October 2026. The weather pattern is expected to last until March 2027 and has already brought drought conditions to various provinces in the country.

articles.title: A part of B.C. now observes the same time as a part of Florida
articles.summary: The Regional District of East Kootenay, which includes B.C. communities like Cranbrook and Kimberley, now observes the same time as Fort Walton Beach and Crestview in Florida.

image.caption: A beach attendant sets up chairs and umbrellas in Fort Walton Beach Fla. — which is now observing the same time zone as Cranbrook, B.C., some 3,200 kilometres away. (Kiichiro Sato/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New
The Regional District of East Kootenay, which includes B.C. communities like Cranbrook and Kimberley, now observes the same time as Fort Walton Beach and Crestview in Florida.
The East Kootenays are on mountain daylight time — which is the same time as central standard time
With B.C. not rolling back its clocks on Sunday, unlike much of the rest of Canada and the U.S., some far-flung communities now share the same time zones — though they may have different names.
Officials in the East Kootenays in southeast B.C. voted in August to stick with Alberta time year-round, which is mountain daylight time, or a permanent UTC−6 time standard.
Part of the Florida Panhandle — more than 3,200 kilometres away — observes central standard time during the winter, which is also UTC-6.
A map of the current time zones across Canada and the U.S. during the winter months. Most of Western Canada did not roll back its clocks on Nov. 1, resulting in many time quirks. (Darius Mahdavi/CBC)

British Columbians woke up on Sunday having not changed their clocks for the first time in decades, and most of B.C. will have to get used to being one hour ahead of Washington state to the south and two hours behind Ontario and much of Quebec this winter.
"All of Eastern Canada, for the most part, besides a small portion of Ontario, did turn back their clocks," said Darius Mahdavi, CBC's science and climate specialist.
"So maybe you woke up and your phone had the wrong time on it because it did fall back when it shouldn't have, maybe your phone and your computer disagreed about what time it was."

items: B.C. won't be changing its clocks on Nov. 1. Here's what you need to know
How daylight hours will shift in B.C. this winter

blocks.text: Those aren't the only quirks that will result from B.C.'s decision not to roll back its clocks last weekend.
Alaska communities will have to adjust to being two hours behind B.C., observing a UTC-9 standard during the winter, despite sharing a large land border.

Meanwhile, residents of Point Roberts, Wash. — a U.S. pene-exclave of Washington state at the southern tip of the Tsawwassen Peninsula, completely cut off by land from the rest of the country — will see their time zones shift by an hour when they cross the border to attend school or access services in Blaine, Wash.
Most of B.C. has now moved to daylight time year-round, a permanent UTC-7 time standard called Pacific time (PT).
The decision to stick with daylight time year-round has prompted criticism from scientists, who said sticking with standard time would have been better for population health overall.
With files from Darius Mahdavi

articles.title: Canada joins coalition refusing to play ice hockey against Russia over Ukraine war
articles.summary:
Growing number of countries are resisting Russia’s reintegration into international hockey after a sports court lifted a ban on competition

Canada has joined a coalition of countries…

blocks.text: Canada has joined a coalition of countries refusing to play ⁠ice ​hockey teams from Russia, with prime minister Mark Carney saying Russian skaters will not be able to compete in ⁠a world junior championship next month due to the war in Ukraine.

“While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified, horrific ‌war in Ukraine, as long as that’s going on, there will be none of ​those athletes competing for their countries in Canada,” Carney told reporters on Tuesday.

Carney’s comments follow announcements by a growing number of national hockey federations that they will not play Russian teams, after ‌a decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) to allow ‌Russians to compete in International Ice Hockey Federation (IHF) events.
An IIHF ban on Russian teams took ⁠effect after Moscow began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and has been extended ​annually.
After several appeals by Russia’s hockey ‌federation, the CAS finally ‌lifted the ban on Friday, contending safety and security worries “were not supported by sufficient evidence”.

On Monday, the Finnish Ice Hockey Association asked other nations to stand up against the decision. Federations representing Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Latvia and the Czech Republic announced Tuesday they sided with Finland.
Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha on Tuesday thanked European nations for “refusing to share the ice with Russia”.

“If CAS lacks a moral compass, let’s show that hockey still has values,” he said in a post on X. “Refuse to play against Russia and deny visas to its players. Keep Russia off the ice! A war of aggression and hockey are incompatible.”
The Norwegians ‌were the first to announce on Tuesday their intention to play games in tournaments against all teams but those involving Russia.
“Our position that Russia should be excluded from all international championships as long as the war in Ukraine continues … remains unchanged,” Norway’s federation posted to social media.

“At this time, this decision is based on our responsibility to ‌protect the safety and wellbeing of our players, team staff and their families. We believe playing against Russia under the current circumstances could expose our players ​and team staff to significant security risks.”
Similar statements followed from the other three nations.
The CAS ruling has left cities worldwide to decide whether they will host upcoming tournaments, as planned, should Russians compete as the war continues in Ukraine.
The world junior ​tournament is scheduled to ​begin 26 December in Alberta.

articles.title: Why Kim Kardashian came back to 'the worst TV drama ever'
articles.summary: The media personality and businesswoman says she's worked on her acting for series two of All's Fair.

blocks.text: "We're a full comedy now," the 46-year-old admits, adding: "The beauty in producing a show with writers that are really tuned in to pop culture is they can see what the response is and write accordingly to that."

All's Fair, which was created by American Horror Story and Glee showrunner Ryan Murphy, became the Hulu network's most-watched scripted series debut of the last three years and was immediately renewed.
Following a group of divorce lawyers - played by Kardashian, Close, Paulson, Naomi Watts and Niecy Nash-Betts - the show was panned for bad acting, with Kardashian baring the brunt of criticism.
The Hollywood Reporter called her "wooden", and the Times declared that the show "may be the worst TV drama ever".

But the hallmark of Kardashian's career has been her ability to back herself - whether that's going from years of being snubbed by Met Gala organisers to becoming its most anticipated guest, or overcoming backlash to the launch of her shapewear company to turn it into a $5bn (£3.7bn) brand.
Kardashian says: "What is the alternative, right? What is the other choice that you have when you're getting criticised?
"Do you just fall in and feel that, or keep your head down and try better, try harder and try a different path?"
Having been in the spotlight for more than 20 years, she's "always had a really good sense of my mental health", and says that comes from being able to "brush off" those who seek to bring her down.
"I always do things that are tough because I genuinely want to learn," Kardashian says.

While she was promoting the legal drama last year, Kardashian was waiting to find out if she had passed exams to become a lawyer in real life, after six years of studying for an apprenticeship that negated the need for a university degree.
Shortly after the first series aired, she found out she had failed the exam - but says that won't be the end of her pursuit of the qualification.
"If I don't pass something, if I don't do the best at something, then I'll get there," she says. "I don't worry. I just have to keep going."
But after her admission that she had used AI for legal advice, external, she does say she will change how public she is about her studies.

"I'm going to be a little more quiet about my journey until I get there," says Kardashian, who has four children with rapper Kanye West and is now in a relationship with British Formula 1 driver Lewis Hamilton.
"I know there was a lot of talk out there like, 'she's given up', and that's funny to me.
"I like people to think what they want to think and I'll take it again and let you guys know once I've passed. I'll be very vocal about that," she says.
Audiences have only been given a glimpse of what to expect from the second series of All's Fair so far.

Co-star Watts, who also serves as a producer on the show alongside Kardashian, says they have "doubled down" on "the high fashion, high drama and heightened reality" that audiences enjoyed the first time around.
As for Kardashian's acting, Watts says she's on a "trajectory" that sees her "stepping up in the second season".
"She was improvising, riffing, doing all kind of things that I thought were deeply impressive," Watts adds, to which Kardashian jokes: "I think I'm just naturally so funny."

One of the positives that critics did cite was the show's desire to spotlight the duality of professional women who were both feminine and successful, which Kardashian says she "loves" because it is "a really realistic depiction of a lot of women I know".
"It doesn't mean that just because you're super smart that you can't be fashionable and into glamorous things as well," she adds.

articles.title: US to cut nearly $4 billion in Israel military aid, Trump says
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said that the United States would still sell weapons to Israel. He added that Democratic candidates were using US military support for Israel against Republicans in the midterm…

image.caption: Trump's surprise announcement came amid the US midterm elections [FILE: December 2025]Image: Jonathan Ernst/REUTERS

blocks.text: The US will end an agreement that sees it provide Israel nearly $4 billion (€3.5 billion) in annual aid by the end of the year, President Donald Trump said Tuesday.
In an interview with the conservative US broadcaster Fox, Trump said Israel was "fine" with him ending the assistance, which is due to run until the end of 2028.

"Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping," Trump told the hosts of the "Fox & Friends" morning show, referring to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump said Israel is "fine" with the US slashing the aid.

"We've already agreed that by the end of the year we won't be paying Israel. Now we'll help Israel if they need it," the US president said, while adding that Israel can still buy US weapons "whenever they want."
"Israel's our number one; we give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it," Trump added.
How much does the US support Israel?
The US provides $3.8 billion to Israel under a 10-year security assistance accord that began in 2019 and was signed by Barack Obama before Trump took office in 2017.

In the Fox News interview, Trump did not elaborate on how the military assistance would end by the end of 2026. The Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) that supplies Israel with nearly $4 billion in military aid each year is set to run until September 2028.

The US has backed Israel far more than any other country. Israel has received the inflation-adjusted equivalent of more than $300 billion in US economic and military support since it was founded in 1948, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.

Netanyahu has said previously that he wants to end Israel's reliance on US military support. In June, he said that while he "deeply" appreciates the support Israel has received from its "American friends … we need to break free from dependency and build our own independent armaments network."
Trump's announcement has drawn fierce criticism from Netanyahu's opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, who is vying to form a coalition that can challenge the prime minister.
The leader of the Israeli opposition said Trump's remarks were evidence that Netanyahu must be removed from office.

"The fact that Israel's defense establishment is learning of a shift in our strategic relationship through the media, at the same time as the Israeli public, shows just how dangerous Benjamin Netanyahu's conduct is," Eisenkot said in a statement posted on X.
"He can no longer be trusted and must be replaced."
Why did Trump make the remarks on midterm election day?

Trump's surprise comments came as US voters headed to polling stations on Tuesday for the midterm elections, which have been framed as a referendum on Trump's second term and could see his Republican Party lose control of Congress.
Democrats such as Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan have criticized continued US aid to Israel while Americans struggle to keep up with rising prices at home.

The US' unconditional support for Israel, which had been a rare and reliable source of bipartisan consensus for decades, has grown increasingly unpopular with the American public, particularly since Israel's military offensive in Gaza, which came in response to the Hamas terror attack in October 2023.

A Quinnipiac University poll in June found that 48% of all voters and 66% of Democrats think the US is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% and 20% in 2017, respectively. A poll by the Pew Research Center in March last year found that 53% of Americans view Israel unfavorably, up from 42% in 2022.

Trump said his move to end aid to Israel was in part meant to counter a "bad talking point" that left-wing Democrats such as El-Sayed have used against Republicans amid rising anti-Israel sentiment in the country over the conflict and humanitarian situation in Gaza.
"Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they (Israel) don't need it (the assistance)?" the US president said on Fox & Friends.
Is Israel running out of friends?
What did Trump say about the war in Iran?
In the same TV interview, Trump also confirmed that US forces attacked Iran overnight.
Trump said the US military hit an Iranian anti-aircraft facility in a "minor" attack.
"They built an anti-aircraft facility... As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night very nicely," Trump told the hosts of the "Fox & Friends" morning show.
The war with Iran, which the US has fought jointly with Israel, has seen US gasoline prices surge and Trump's approval ratings decline sharply as a result.
Jon Alterman of the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank in Washington, told Reuters news agency that the timing of Trump's announcements on Israel and Iran was "curious."
"Why did President Trump announce it on Election Day? And why did he announce ​it amidst speculation that a major joint US-Israeli military strike against Iran may be ⁠days away?"
US strikes Iran hours before midterm election

articles.title: B.C. privacy watchdog launches investigation into Crime Stoppers data breach
articles.summary: B.C.'s privacy watchdog has launched an investigation into whether the provincial Crime Stoppers society took adequate steps to protect personal information following a massive data breach that…

image.caption: A CBC News investigation found more than 1.5 million tips submitted to Crime Stoppers programs across the country over the past 25 years were compromised. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

B.C.'s privacy watchdog has launched an investigation into whether the provincial Crime Stoppers society took adequate steps to protect personal information following a massive data breach that exposed more than 1.5 million anonymous crime tips across Canada.
It comes after a CBC investigation revealed that over 1.5 million tips submitted anonymously were leaked

B.C.'s privacy watchdog has launched an investigation into whether the provincial Crime Stoppers society took adequate steps to protect personal information following a massive data breach across Canada.

The Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner for B.C. (OIPC) announced Tuesday that it's investigating whether the B.C. Crime Stoppers met its obligation under the Personal Information Protection Act to take reasonable steps to safeguard the personal information it holds.
Last month, an exclusive CBC investigation found more than 1.5 million tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years were exposed in a massive data breach.

The data was stolen last March by hacktivist collective Internet Yiff Machine. In a manifesto, the group said it wanted to disprove the claim by P3 Global Intel — the company hired by Crime Stoppers to manage its tips — that the platform was "anonymous" and "secure."
More Canadian Crime Stoppers chapters pause program after CBC investigation | Hanomansing Live

Crime Stoppers is a network of civilian-run non-profits that collects anonymous tips on crime and suspicious activity. It operates independently of law enforcement, though it refers a portion of tips back to them to assist in investigations.

The organization often appeals to the public, in partnership with police, for help with unsolved crimes and to advance investigations — all with the promise of anonymity for tipsters who contact them.
Many of the compromised tips dealt with serious allegations, with some people explicitly saying they feared retribution for speaking out.

A third of all tips talked about drugs and drug trafficking; hundreds reported suspicious activity in their neighbourhoods, often naming individuals and implicating organized crime, biker gangs or drug cartels — including the Hells Angels, Rock Machine and Outlaws, as well as B.C.’s Red Scorpions and Independent Soldiers.

items: Canadian Crime Stoppers Association advises chapters to accept tips by phone only

blocks.text: The breach has prompted several police agencies and Crime Stoppers chapters across Canada to temporarily suspend their participation or stop accepting tips.
Metro Vancouver Crime Stoppers has posted a notice on its website asking people not to submit information through its program until further notice.
"This pause is temporary. We will begin accepting new tips as soon as we are confident it is safe to do so," the organization said.
It is directing people with information about crimes to contact their local police departments instead.
According to B.C. Crime Stoppers, 15 volunteer-driven chapters operate across the province.
The OIPC says people who believe their information may have been compromised do not need to file individual complaints because of the sensitive nature of the data involved.
The watchdog said it could not provide further details while its investigation remains active.
The federal privacy commissioner has also previously announced his office is looking into the breach.
With files from Valérie Ouellet and Michelle Allan

articles.title: ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline
articles.summary: As South Africans vote in local elections, residents tell the BBC they are tired of the poor quality of services they get.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
More than 500 parties are contesting the elections
ByKhanyisile Ngcobo
Reporting fromJohannesburg
South Africans are voting in highly contested local elections likely to see a haemorrhaging of votes for the country's former ruling party, the African National Congress (ANC).
This year's voting season has been marked by intense campaigns that have included politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and even wading through giant-sized potholes.
Leaders are campaigning to head South Africa's nearly 300 municipalities, responsible for basic service provision such as water, electricity and refuse collection.

For the ANC, the elections are a chance to prove it still has what it takes to govern. The party had a disastrous showing in the last national election, when it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since 1994 when the racist apartheid system ended.
Support for the party has been dropping significantly over the years because of anger over high levels of corruption, unemployment and crime.
At its peak, in 2004, the ANC got 70% of the vote in the general election. Two decades later its share dropped to 40%.
Polls and pundits have predicted a further loss in these elections but President Cyril Ramaphosa has denied that his party was in a downward spiral.
"What I'm seeing here is that the ANC is going higher and higher and on the 4th [of November] we will show those naysayers," he told supporters at the party's final election rally on Sunday.
In townships like Alexandra, north-east of Johannesburg, the ANC has traditionally had a strong supporter base but poor governance and voter apathy are unravelling this support.

The BBC visited the sprawling township a week before the elections and spoke to residents to get their views. One of them was Sanele Ntombela, who is a first-time voter excited to make his voice heard.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Sanele Ntombela (left), seen here with his friends Tshiamo Mbange (centre) and Lwandle Dladla, is excited to cast his vote

blocks.text: Image source, Khanyisile Ngcobo/BBC
Sanele Ntombela (left), seen here with his friends Tshiamo Mbange (centre) and Lwandle Dladla, is excited to cast his vote
We found the 18-year-old hanging out with his friends on a street corner. Most of his friends said they had no intention of voting and had not registered to do so.
They cited a lack of change and deteriorating delivery of basic services.
But Ntombela was looking forward to voting for the first time and thought it might lead to change.
"We face many challenges in Alexandra. There's rubbish everywhere and we struggle with electricity and water and many other issues," he said.
Just metres away, heaps of rubbish lay gathered beneath a streetlight pole covered in election posters from the different political parties.
On the other side of the street, drain water trickles through the many potholes that have gutted that part of the road.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The ANC faces immense pressure to reverse years of decline

blocks.text: The ANC faces immense pressure to reverse years of decline
The BBC also spoke to Zandile Mncube, who said she wouldn't vote, even though she is registered to do so.
The 33-year-old woman also cited poor service delivery and performance by local leaders for her decision.
"It makes no difference [whether I vote or not]. Things have gotten worse over the years," she said.
Alex, as the township is known, is a stone's throw away from Sandton, Africa's richest square mile, but the differences could not be starker.

Sandton is known for its skyscrapers, designer shops and well-maintained roads but in Alex, houses are sandwiched together and rubbish, either piled together or left strewn across the pavement, is everywhere. The stench of raw sewage and uncollected rubbish is heavy in the air, but residents appear used to it.
The issues plaguing Alexandra are not unique. A drive around Gauteng province reveals similar patterns of neglect and disrepair, especially in the townships.
South of Johannesburg, Soweto looks marginally cleaner than Alexandra, but residents also complain about service delivery.
Mduduzi Makhubo, 45, has lived in Soweto his entire life and he told the BBC of the community's daily struggles with accessing water and electricity.
"Every Monday we know we won't have water after 2pm," he said.
Makhubo is registered to vote and intends to use his vote to deal with the "arrogance" he says local leaders have towards residents and "change the status quo".
These areas offer a small, but important, glimpse into the state of South Africa's local governance.
Years of reports by the auditor-general have highlighted the dire state of most of South Africa's 257 municipalities.

A recent report only gave 39 clean audits - the highest ranking a public entity can achieve - between 2024 and 2025. None of Gauteng's three metro cities, Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni, featured in this list.
Earlier this year auditor-general Tsakani Maluleke said Johannesburg "needs ongoing attention".

"If we don't that, we are going to continue on this slide where financial health deteriorates [and] where service delivery continues to be compromised, which is what we are living," she told lawmakers.
The city has been labelled "effectively bankrupt" due to the dire state of its finances. Dirty streets, unstable electricity supply and persistent water issues have been common for years.

Experts the BBC spoke to agreed that all eyes will be on Africa's wealthiest city as well as the country's seven other biggest municipalities, or metros, particularly those in Gauteng when the results come in.

blocks.caption: Political analyst Melanie Verwoerd is seen smiling with a denim jacket

blocks.text: Melanie Verwoerd
The expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done

blocks.caption: "The expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done", Source: Melanie Verwoerd, Source description: Political analyst, Image: Political analyst Melanie Verwoerd is seen smiling with a denim jacket

blocks.text: Of South Africa's eight metros, only three are governed by a single party. In Gauteng, all three metros are governed by coalition governments, with the ANC the largest party.
But that might change.
Political analyst Melanie Verwoerd said the elections would be a "verdict ... and judgment" on the ANC.
"And the expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done," she said.
Several polls point to a continued decline in support for the party in Wednesday's election, contested by over 500 political parties.
One, conducted by Ipsos, put the ANC's support at 30%, down from the 46% it got at the last local elections in 2021.

The same poll, along with others, points to a slight increase in electoral support for the Democratic Alliance (DA), especially in Johannesburg. Ipsos predicts the DA will garner 25% support in this election, up from 22% last time.
DA leader Helen Zille has been vying for the mayoral chain in the city and her unusual campaign has attracted a lot of attention.

The former Cape Town mayor has been captured swimming in crater-sized potholes, ziplining over sinkholes and riding into her final rally in the city in a classic BMW 325i, known locally as a "Gusheshe".
She believes the DA is the country's best choice for a government, telling local radio broadcaster 702 last week that "towns and cities that work best are under DA governance".
Verwoerd, a former ANC MP and South Africa's ambassador to Ireland, predicted that coalitions would continue being the order of the day across Gauteng.

These types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic at a local level and the constant change in leadership, usually caused by parties falling out with each other, has affected service delivery in many municipalities.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zandile Mncube says things have got worse in her township over the years

blocks.text: Zandile Mncube says things have got worse in her township over the years
Verwoerd said in her view, the most stable coalitions would be those that replicate what the ANC and DA have done on a national level, where the historic rivals have agreed to share power.

Reflecting on Cape Town, she said it was unlikely that the DA would lose control of the municipality. The coastal city is widely considered the country's best-performing metro and has been run by the DA since the late 2000s when it unseated the ANC.
Ethekwini, which includes the port city of Durban in KwaZulu-Natal, would be a "different story", Verwoerd said.

The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party has been projected to perform well in the area but it is unclear if it will secure the outright majority needed to run the metro. Polls suggest it won't and will need partners to form a government.
The party was founded by former South African President Jacob Zuma and was the biggest party across his home province of KwaZulu-Natal in the 2024 provincial election.
Verwoerd reflected that while various options were on the table for the party, forming a government would be "very messy" given its refusal to work with either the ANC or DA.
A confident Zuma, addressing supporters on Sunday, vowed to take control of a number of municipalities after the elections.
Another political analyst Dr Levy Ndou echoed Verwoerd's assessment, saying that a coalition between the DA and ANC seemed unavoidable in most metros.
"We're not sure whether the arrangement of the government of national unity could have the potential to influence how the metros are going to be run," he said.

Both experts also spoke about the declining voter turnout in South Africa's elections. Over 29 million citizens are registered to vote, but the turnout, especially among young people, has seen a steady decline.

Ndou attributed this to the "calibre" of the candidates campaigning and the lack of visibility of local councillors, who are often the ones elected to lead their neighbourhoods, in election campaigns.
South Africa's electoral commission has seven days to announce the results, but parties have 14 days to form a governing structure.

articles.title: Houses of Parliament at risk of ‘Notre Dame-style fire’ as renovation costs rise
articles.summary:
Report says cost of maintenance could soon reach £2m a week, including 24-hour patrols to avert fire risk

The Palace of Westminster will be at risk of a Notre Dame-style fire or a similar…

blocks.text: The Palace of Westminster will be at risk of a Notre Dame-style fire or a similar catastrophic event if MPs do not tackle the issue of funding refurbishments, a parliamentary committee has said.

Decisions about how and when to begin a full restoration of the building, which is Grade I-listed and a Unesco world heritage site, have been repeatedly delayed amid disagreement over how it should be done and spiralling costs.
The cost of maintaining the estate will soon hit £2m a week, and a recent estimate found the work could cost as much as £40bn and potentially last for six decades.

The cross-party Commons public accounts committee (PAC) said urgent action was needed to avoid the risk of a major fire or similar disaster, and to staunch increasing costs, with every year of inaction adding an estimated £420m to the restoration programme.
There has been a “political allergy” to making decisions, Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, the Conservative MP who chairs the PAC, said.
As well as the ever-increasing costs, he said, MPs should also “imagine the blow suffered by the UK’s morale and reputation of some kind of catastrophic failure”.

“Consider the impact of global rolling news footage of Notre Dame-like flames licking out of the building’s roof, resulting in the destruction of our heritage, or worse, injuries or loss of life,” he said.
“These are not notional possibilities, but real and rising risks.”

The Victorian estate has been beset by problems that are barely kept in check by ongoing maintenance, including regular plumbing failures, leaking roofs, crumbling masonry protected by a maze of scaffolding and a persistent risk of fire, mainly from outdated electrics, necessitating 24-hour fire patrols.
This has resulted in a maintenance bill of about £1.5m a week. The PAC report said that without action the figure was expected to reach £2m.

The issue has been seen as a matter for MPs and peers for decide, rather than the government. The PAC stressed that it was not its role to recommend a particular programme, but the report urges action and has made a series of recommendations for making the process work better.

It says that in the next six months the clerks of the Commons and the Lords – who are nominally in charge of the process – should set out a plan to properly engage parliamentarians, something it says has so far been lacking.

Other recommendations include a more robust set of cost estimates and a timetable to help a decision about the main project in 2030, as well as a more urgent approach to finalising temporary accommodation for both chambers while the works take place.

Calling the current governance of the scheme “far too complex”, it says it should be made easier, and a new restoration and renewal select committee formed, allowing MPs to hold senior officials to account.
after newsletter promotion

Four proposals for refurbishment, ranging from a nearly-full exit from the estate during the works to a version in which only the Lords would move, have been narrowed to two, from which MPs must choose.

The first, a “full decant”, would involve staff moving to buildings on the north side of the estate, with the Commons being put in Richmond House, a nearby government building, and the Lords to the QEII conference centre. The project would last up to 24 years and cost about £15.6bn.
A “staged decant” would last anything from 38 to 61 years and involve the Commons moving to the Lords chamber for up to two years. That project would cost about £39.2bn.
The report says there are particular worries about the temporary accommodation in terms of ensuring it is available and the cost.

It states that the estimate to refurbish the QEII centre of £417m, and a bill of about £2bn to set up the northern part of the estate for a decant, feel “very high”, noting that Canada had managed to install a temporary chamber as its parliamentary estate was refurbished for much less.
“We are concerned that the programme is being shaped around the availability of temporary accommodation, rather than temporary accommodation being delivered to meet the programme’s needs,” it said.
A parliament spokesperson said the report “provides welcome scrutiny”.

“The PAC concludes that without action, the Palace of Westminster will, at best, be in a process of managed decline,” they said. “Work is already happening across the parliamentary estate to ensure the ongoing safety of those working here and visiting.”

articles.title: Wage hikes in Western Visayas, Soccsksargen take effect Nov. 19
articles.summary: How much will workers earn under new Western Visayas, SOCCSKSARGEN wage hikes?

blocks.text: November 4, 2026 | 8:00am

At least 300,000 workers in Regions 6 and 10 will receive daily wage hikes computed based on cost of living, inflation and the Philippine peso's purchasing power, according to the National Wages and Productivity Commission's (NWPC).
Philstar.com / Irra Lising

MANILA, Philippines — More than 300,000 minimum wage earners in Western Visayas and Soccsksargen will receive higher pay beginning November 19 following the approval of new wage orders by the National Wages and Productivity Commission.
Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino said the wage boards considered factors such as the cost of living, inflation and the purchasing power of the peso in determining the increases.
The boards also considered workers' needs and employers' capacity to pay.
Western Visayas. Workers in Western Visayas will receive daily wage increases ranging from P40 to P45.
Nonagricultural workers in establishments with more than 10 employees will receive P590 per day, up from P550.
Those in establishments with 10 workers or fewer will receive P565 per day, up from P525, while agricultural workers will also receive P565, up from P520.
Domestic workers in the region will receive an additional P500 per month, raising their monthly minimum wage from P6,500 to P7,000.
SOCCSKSARGEN. In Soccsksargen, a P41 daily wage increase will be implemented in two tranches.
The first P16 increase will take effect on November 19, raising the daily minimum wage to P476 for nonagricultural, retail and service workers and P459 for agricultural workers.
A second increase of P25 will take effect on January 1, 2027, bringing the rates to P501 and P484, respectively.
Domestic workers in SOCCSKSARGEN will receive a P450 monthly increase beginning November 19, raising their minimum wage from P6,000 to P6,450.

articles.title: Myanmar nationals ask Philippines' appeals court to act on stalled war crimes case
articles.summary: Chin war survivors want the DOJ compelled to act on their 2023 complaint.

blocks.text: November 4, 2026 | 7:30am
This composite photo depicts the flag of Myanmar, which the military regime has controlled since seizing power in 2021.
Graphics by Philstar.com / Anjilica Andaya

MANILA, Philippines — Myanmar nationals who survived the civil war in Chin State have asked the Court of Appeals to compel Philippine authorities to act on their war crimes complaint against members of Myanmar's military junta.

The petitioners filed a petition for certiorari and mandamus on November 3, asking the appellate court to order action on their pending motion for reconsideration, formally docket their 2023 complaint-affidavit and proceed with a preliminary investigation.
They are also seeking to nullify a February 2024 letter from the Department of Justice and what they described as subsequent "implied denials" of their complaint.

Through the petition for mandamus, the survivors asked Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida and Prosecutor General Richard Anthony Fadullon to conduct a preliminary investigation into the alleged war crimes.

Named as respondents in the complaint are Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, Vung Suan Thang, Lt. General Tay Zar Kyaw, Maj. General Phyo Thant, Maj. General Than Htike, Brig. General Myo Htut Hlaing, Col. Saw Thun, Lt. Col. Myo Zin Tun and Major Nay Myo Oo.

The survivors first sought help from Philippine authorities in 2024, arguing that Republic Act 9851 allows Philippine courts to hear war crimes and crimes against humanity cases involving acts committed abroad, under certain conditions.

The DOJ previously declined to act on the complaint because neither the victims nor the accused are Filipino and the respondents are not in the Philippines. The survivors argue, however, that the principle of universal jurisdiction still requires Philippine authorities to at least investigate the alleged war crimes.
'Three years of silence'
Lawyer Rommel Bagares said the petition seeks to enforce the survivors' constitutional right to the speedy disposition of cases and due process.
"The right to the speedy disposition of cases is not a courtesy. It is a guarantee written into Article III, Section 16 of our Constitution," Bagares said.
"Three years of silence is not neutrality. For a displaced population whose witnesses are aging, every month of delay is prejudice," he added.
Lawyer Gilbert Andres, meanwhile, invoked Section 17 of the Philippine Act on Crimes Against International Humanitarian Law, Genocide, and Other Crimes Against Humanity.
"If Section 17 is robust enough for the State to wield in other cases, it cannot be too weak for these Chin victims to invoke in theirs," Andres said.
Andres and other lawyers filed a motion to resolve with the DOJ on July 31 after the complaint had remained pending since 2023.
The Chin survivors, through Andres and Bagares, filed the complaint invoking "universal jurisdiction" over alleged war crimes.

articles.title: P.E.I. Premier Rob Lantz facing pressure to step down
articles.summary: A formal petition signed by members of the P.E.I. Progressive Conservative Party is calling for a vote on Premier Rob Lantz's leadership.

blocks.text: PEI·New
A formal petition signed by members of the P.E.I. Progressive Conservative Party is calling for a vote on Premier Rob Lantz's leadership.
Petition from party members is asking for a special meeting to be held in next 15 days
P.E.I. Premier Rob Lantz faces calls for leadership review
A formal petition signed by some members of the P.E.I. Progressive Conservative Party is calling for a vote on Premier Rob Lantz's leadership.
Lantz secured his position as party leader and premier following a leadership contest win in February over Mark Ledwell with 53.1 per cent of the vote.
Martie Murphy, a longtime member of the party, said the petition is currently signed by more than 120 members. She said some in the party have become discouraged.
"We feel like doing nothing is political demise because we're not going to climb up in the polls with the leadership the way that it is," she said.

"It's really everybody. It's a combination of rural, city. So it's everybody that has a concern where the Island sits right now. The leadership is in question. They have lost the confidence from Islanders and party members."
PC Party member Martie Murphy says the petition is currently signed by more than 120 party members. She says some in the party have become discouraged. (Steve Bruce/CBC)
The petition and resolution, sent to the party association, is asking for a special general meeting for voting on the issue to be held within the next 15 days.
Lantz would have an opportunity to speak at the meeting, and members would vote by secret ballot on whether they want him to step down. Then, it would be up to Lantz to decide next steps.
'Weak public support'

The resolution notes concerns regarding financial responsibility as well as transparency and accountability, pointing to the province's "rapidly escalating and unsustainable deficit," and says there are "significant questions about the current leadership and its ability to responsibly manage the Province's financial affairs."

It goes on to state that the PC Party "continues to experience historically weak public support, with no meaningful improvement reflected in consecutive polls, demonstrating a growing loss of confidence not only among party members but across the electorate, placing the party's future electoral viability and its ability to form government at serious risk."

items: Why P.E.I.'s fall legislature sitting could be the most consequential in years for all 3 parties
Lantz says he’s still the right leader as P.E.I. plans major future investments

blocks.text: Lantz said he is aware the party has received the petition and he will "let the party work through that."
He added the party has more than 7,200 members and that, under its constitution, it takes 75 signatures to compel a leadership vote.
"That's a pretty low bar. But in the meantime, I'm just focused on the work of government and the priorities of Islanders," he said.
"Yes, this is a distraction, but I'm focused on the work that I was elected to do."
P.E.I. Premier Rob Lantz says he feels there is 'a small number of people' who never accepted the results of the leadership convention earlier this year. (Rick Gibbs/CBC)
Lantz said he feels there is "a small number of people" who never accepted the results of the leadership convention and they are "trying to compel a discussion."
"It appears to me they just want to roll back the clock to reverse a democratic decision that was made by this party, but it is what it is," he said.
"We'll go through this process, but then people are going to have to move on and focus on working for Islanders."

PC Party president Robert Larsen confirmed via email the party received a petition requesting a special general meeting but did not say when such a meeting may happen or if a vote on Lantz's leadership would occur.
He said the party is consulting legal counsel on what is now required under the party constitution.

Questions regarding Lantz's leadership were brought up in the legislature during question period Tuesday, with Liberal Opposition Leader Hal Perry stating the province is facing "many serious challenges," adding "it is so sad that the source of many of these difficulties is the provincial government."
Liberal Opposition Leader Hal Perry said during question period that the province is facing 'many serious challenges' and pointed to the government as the source. (P.E.I. Legislative Assembly)

"Rather than leading with a clear vision and plan, this government stumbles from one mistake to another. Instead of substance, it's photo-ops and Facebook rather than policy and pocketbooks," Perry said.
"This province has not had the opportunity to endorse this premier or his plans and yet this premier is making incredibly long-term and potentially damaging decisions."
Lantz responded to Perry that Islanders elected the Progressive Conservative government "with a strong majority" and that it is "delivering on that mandate every day."
"Islanders want us focused on access to care, on the price at the pump, protecting jobs from tariffs, and that's what we're doing," Lantz said.
"They don't want us focused on an election right now. We're delivering on a mandate that we were given and that's what we'll continue to do."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Lucas McInnis is a journalist at CBC Prince Edward Island. He can be reached at lucas.mcinnis@cbc.ca.
With files from Steve Bruce

articles.title: Carney says U.S. 'asking less and offering more' with 'more intense' trade talks underway
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada and the U.S. have made progress on reaching a trade deal, but stressed more work is needed before any agreement is finalized.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney is seen at the Commonwealth summit on Tuesday in St. John's, Antigua and Barbuda, where he said progress is being made in U.S. trade negotiations. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada and the U.S. have made progress on reaching a trade deal, but stressed more work is needed before any agreement is finalized.
Some of Canada's red lines now seen by U.S. as off the table: PM

"They're asking less and they're offering more, but we're not quite there," Carney said of the state of negotiations while on the sidelines of meeting with other Commonwealth leaders in Antigua on Tuesday.
After trade talks collapsed dramatically in August, Carney said "more intense negotiations" have since begun.
The prime minister attributed that to the White House's position shifting on some of Canada's "red lines."
'We've made progress' with U.S. on trade talks, Carney says

When talks fell apart over the summer, the Canadian side said U.S. negotiators took issue with rules that ensure French-language content is easy to find on streaming platforms, such as Netflix, and that the Americans tried to restrict Canada's ability to strike trade deals with other countries.
"Those are now off the table. That's very welcome," said Carney.
The progress, as the prime minister described it, on the trade file comes as Trump's Republican Party faces what could be a tough midterm showing.

items: Carney has 'good conversation' with Trump on future of Canada-U.S. trade as midterms near

blocks.text: Pollsters have been expecting a blue wave as American voters increasingly voice frustrations about the cost of living, driven in part by the war in Iran and tariffs, in the lead up to Tuesday's vote.
In an interview Tuesday morning, Trump told Fox News that his administration was nearing a trade agreement with Canada.
While Carney didn't outline what issues remain, autos are expected to be a key sticking point, as they were in August before talks collapsed — triggering new tariffs on both sides.
Carney said he'll meet Trump in China later this month at the APEC summit.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Catharine Tunney is a reporter with CBC's Parliament Hill bureau, where she covers national security and the RCMP. She worked previously for CBC in Nova Scotia. You can reach her at catharine.tunney@cbc.ca

blocks.text: What early races could indicate a blue wave? Here's where were watching.
Chris Hippensteel

As polls begin to close on election night, some early House and Senate races could indicate which way the election is trending – whether Democrats are set for the blowout they’re hoping for, or whether Republicans will defy the polls and hold onto control of Congress.
There’s a strong possibility we won’t have an idea which party will come out on top until tomorrow or later this week. But these states might provide some early signs (timings are in ET):

blocks.text: Americans vote in midterms that will determine control of Congress and Trump’s agenda

It’s almost 6pm ET on Tuesday 3 November, and the first round of polls in the US midterm elections are about to close. After months of campaigning, debate and analysis, Americans have been casting their ballots in these critical elections that will take the political temperature of the nation halfway through Donald Trump’s second term – and determine the trajectory of the remainder of his presidency.

Americans, who have already voted early in record numbers and are turning out in numbers significantly outstripping the totals from the 2022 midterms, will decide the balance of power in Congress and, therefore, Trump’s ability to advance his agenda for the next two years.

With the US president almost unprecedentedly unpopular, Democrats are aiming for what would be stunning victories in seats where, for decades, turning blue would have been unthinkable. Trump is not on the ballot, but this election is very much a referendum on the direction of the country under his Republican party.
Results will soon begin trickling in for what will be a defining moment for American democracy, so stick with us as we bring you all the latest news, analyses and commentary as it all unfolds.

articles.title: PM, Manitoba premier only ones to bring up abolishing Indian Act at meeting: AFN chief
articles.summary: The national chief of the Assembly of First Nations says the only leaders to discuss abolishing the Indian Act during a landmark meeting last week were Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew and Prime Minister…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney listens as Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak answers a question at a meeting in Ottawa last week. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New

The national chief of the Assembly of First Nations says the only leaders to discuss abolishing the Indian Act during a landmark meeting last week were Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew and Prime Minister Mark Carney.
Major projects conversation 'went to the wayside' after remarks at historic summit, Woodhouse Nepinak says
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 03, 2026 5:48 PM EST | Last Updated: 4 minutes ago
Carney said after the meeting that the idea was raised by chiefs in the room.
Kinew, who is Anishinaabe, called for the act to be abolished during the historic gathering of federal, provincial and First Nations leaders in Ottawa.

The Indian Act, which dates back to 1876, gives Ottawa sweeping powers over First Nations communities and people, including the authority to decide who qualifies for status and what reserves can and can't do.

Both Kinew and Carney said the idea to change or abolish the Indian Act was raised and supported by some chiefs in the room. Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said on Tuesday that that's not true.

Woodhouse Nepinak said the chiefs were focused more on the major projects legislation they say threatens their rights, and that those conversations "went to the wayside" when Kinew and Carney made their remarks.
The prime minister said after the meeting that he was "very open to" the idea but later said the Indian Act could be reformed rather than abolished.

"Not everybody, but other participants raised the desirability. So, it's already starting from the right place in that it's not the federal government deciding something should be done. It's responding to a request," Carney said at the time.
A spokesperson for Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty says Kinew wasn't the only one to bring up the Indian Act at the gathering. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

A spokesperson for federal Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty's office said in an emailed statement Friday that Kinew was not the only person to raise the possibility of reforming or removing the Indian Act at the meeting.
"As the meeting was held behind closed doors, it would be inappropriate to provide more specificity on the details of the conversation," Livi McElrea said.

items: 'Time to abolish the Indian Act,' Manitoba premier tells PM in historic meeting with chiefs
'Healthy' to have conversation on abolishing Indian Act, First Nation chief says

blocks.text: While First Nations chiefs generally agree the law is outdated and restrictive, there is little consensus on whether it should be repealed and what might take its place.
First Nations leaders broadly support changing the rules on how the Indian Act determines who qualifies for status. The federal government has not committed to changing those rules.

Previous prime ministers have tried and failed to reform or eliminate the Indian Act. In 1969, years before he became prime minister, Jean Chrétien introduced what was known as the White Paper when he was Indian Affairs minister in Pierre Trudeau's government.

The document called for the abolition of the Indian Act, an end to Indian status, the absorption of First Nations people as ordinary Canadian citizens, the termination of treaties and the privatization of reserve lands.

The proposal received widespread pushback from First Nations leaders, led in part by Harold Cardinal and the Indian Association of Alberta. They called Chrétien's plan assimilationist and warned it would lead to the erasure of their cultures.

items: First Nations must lead Indian Act reform, Onion Lake Cree Nation chief says
Some First Nations leaders in B.C. push back against Kinew's calls

blocks.text: In the emailed statement from Gull-Masty's office, McElrea said Carney has acknowledged the Indian Act is racist and that it's necessary to have a broader conversation with First Nations about its future.
There are policies in place if a First Nation decides to opt out of the Indian Act and move toward self-government.

Gull-Masty's community, the Cree First Nation of Waswanipi, is one of those self-governing communities under the 1975 James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement — the first modern land claim in Canada, and one in which Chrétien played a leading role.

items: Carney government is stalling on Indian Act reform bill, advocates, lawmakers charge
Métis leaders condemn Assembly of First Nations national chief's remarks in Ottawa

blocks.text: Talk of reforming or abolishing the Indian Act comes as Carney works to speed up development of major projects alongside the provinces and Indigenous people.
His government's Building Canada Act initially gave Ottawa the power to sidestep the Indian Act, but that provision was removed in response to calls from the Conservatives and the Bloc Québécois.

articles.title: New Alberta bill would compel ‘neutrality’ for post-secondary institutions on political issues
articles.summary: Universities will be compelled to stay neutral and allow freedom of expression if the Alberta legislature passes a new bill introduced by the United Conservative government on Tuesday.

image.caption: Alberta Advanced Education Minister Myles McDougall discusses the introduction of Bill 38, the Advanced Education Amendment Act, at a news conference on Tuesday, Nov. 3. (Janet French/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton·Updated
Universities will be compelled to stay neutral and allow freedom of expression if the Alberta legislature passes a new bill introduced by the United Conservative government on Tuesday.
Bill 38 also caps tuition increases at 2% for 2027-28 academic year
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 03, 2026 5:10 PM EST | Last Updated: 21 minutes ago
Universities will be compelled to stay neutral and allow freedom of expression if the Alberta Legislature passes a new bill introduced by the United Conservative government on Tuesday.
Bill 38, the Advanced Education Statutes Amendment Act, 2026, proposes changes to the Post-secondary Learning Act.
Myles McDougall, Alberta’s minister of advanced education, said while institutions have to remain neutral, the same requirement will not apply to individuals within the institution.

“The underlying political reasons why things are happening and the position as to who's right or wrong, et cetera, that is not the role of the institution to take,” McDougall said during a news conference at the Alberta legislature.
“But certainly the people within the post-secondary system — students, faculty [and] administrators — are free to express their opinions.”
This bill follows a high-profile case where the University of Lethbridge cancelled an on-campus lecture by former Mount Royal University professor Frances Widdowson in 2023.
Widdowson is known for expressing controversial views. In 2020, she made headlines for suggesting residential schools provided educational benefits to First Nations children.
In September, a Court of King’s Bench justice ruled that the university was wrong to cancel Widdowson’s lecture.

Bill 38 also aims to cap tuition fee increases at two per cent in 2027-28 for Canadian students attending post-secondary institutions in Alberta. McDougall would not say what will happen in subsequent years.
The bill also establishes minimum standards for student codes of conduct, which will be specified in future regulations.
McDougall announced that Alberta will no longer include parental income when assessing eligibility for student loans.
He said this would free up about $118 million in additional loans within the existing student loan disbursement budget.
Expert panel
In 2025, an expert panel chaired by economist Jack Mintz, made 11 recommendations for the province’s universities, colleges and polytechnics.

The panel recommended the government mandate all public post-secondary institutions to be neutral and maintain freedom of expression. The panel also recommended Alberta update its funding model for post-secondary schools that would take into account enrolment, performance and base funding.
MLA David Eggen, the NDP critic for advanced education, said that McDougall appears to have cherry-picked a couple of aspects of the Mintz report without dealing with funding.
Eggen said many students are having difficulty affording tuition and increases in the cost of living. He said Bill 38 doesn’t help them with that.

“Instead, it's looking for some diversions around culture wars, around code of conduct for students and institutional neutrality — things that mean very little when our advanced education system is already under serious stress from a lack of funding from this government," said Eggen.
The uncertainty of what happens with tuition after the 2027-28 academic year is raising concerns for the Alberta Students' Executive Council (ASEC).
ASEC chair Rylee Mae, a student at the University of Lethbridge, said even if tuition fee increases are capped, tuition can still remain unaffordable for students.
"A tuition ceiling still needs safeguards on how quickly tuition can rise, so students need to be able to plan for the cost of completing their education," she said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Michelle Bellefontaine covers the Alberta legislature for CBC News in Edmonton. She has also worked as a reporter in the Maritimes and in northern Canada.

articles.title: One dead and another missing in suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
articles.summary:
The incident took place in the same province where a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren last November

A mother is dead and her daughter is missing in western Canada after a suspected…

blocks.text: A mother is dead and her daughter is missing in western Canada after a suspected grizzly bear attack in the same community where a bear attacked a group of schoolchildren earlier in the year.

On Tuesday, the British Columbia conservation officer service said in a social media post that it had launched a search for the two missing people on the weekend, and that during the search on Sunday an officer found the mother’s body. The search for her 19-year-old daughter is ongoing.
“Our thoughts are with the families of the victims during this tragic time,” Inspector Jeff Tyre said in a video posted online.

Jenny Balcarras, an art therapist, and her daughter were reported missing by relatives over the weekend. A family member posted on Facebook about them, later updating it after the conservation service announced the suspected attack to indicate that their vehicle had been found at a trailhead near Bella Coola, British Columbia.
The suspected attack happened at the Snooka West trail area, about 8km (4.97 miles) east of Bella Coola, on the province’s central coast.

Bella Coola, a community of roughly 2,100 people, sits at the end of a fjord along the province’s central coast. Its remote location and abundant food sources mean that grizzly bears are a common sight in the region, which is informally known as the Great Bear rainforest.

Grizzly attacks in the province are exceedingly rare, but last November, 11 people, some as young as nine years old, were injured when a grizzly emerged from the forest near 4 Mile, a Nuxalk community, and attacked a school group on a lunch break alongside a walking trail. Despite an extensive search, the bear was never located.

“While the full circumstances are still unfolding, we understand first-hand the trauma this incident will inflict upon the victims’ family members, the victims of last year’s attack and the community at large,” said Samuel Schooner, elected chief of the Nuxalk Nation, on Tuesday. “Our thoughts are with the victim’s family as they learn of this tragic event.”
Schooner said a trapping effort to find the bear was under way and asked media to refrain from contacting community members.

articles.title: Reform UK councillor charged with 12 counts of rape and multiple other offences
articles.summary:
George Madgwick, party leader on Hampshire county council, faces charges related to four teenagers between 2008 and 2021

Reform UK’s leader on Hampshire county council has been charged with…

blocks.text: Reform UK’s leader on Hampshire county council has been charged with 12 counts of rape and one of distributing indecent images of a child.

George Madgwick, 37, who is a councillor in Portsmouth and leads the Reform group on the council, was a prominent voice linked to recent protests in the town connected to the arrival of asylum seekers on small boats.

A Crown Prosecution Service statement said the charges followed a police investigation into allegations connected to four complainants, aged 16 and 17 at the time, and were alleged to have taken place in Portsmouth and Wales between 2008 and 2021. On 6 January, officers arrested a man at an address in Wandsworth, London.

The charges comprise 12 allegations of rape; eight of actual bodily harm; two of assault by penetration; two of sexual assault; two of controlling and coercive behaviour; two of making an indecent image of a child; one of distribution of an indecent image of a child; one of stalking; one of making threats to kill; one of false imprisonment; one of criminal damage; one of theft; and one of causing or inciting the sexual exploitation of a child.

Madgwick is scheduled to appear at Portsmouth magistrates court on 25 November. A CPS spokesperson said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute George Madgwick for serious sexual offences, including multiple counts of rape. He has also been charged with making a threat to kill, false imprisonment and stalking.
“Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence and that it is in the public interest to bring the case to court.

“We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are now active and that he has the right to a fair trial. There should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings.”
A Reform spokesperson said: “Cllr Madgwick has been suspended from Reform UK with immediate effect.”

Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said: “These charges are truly shocking. Nigel Farage must urgently tell the public whether he was aware of Councillor Madgwick’s arrest, or of any of the appalling allegations he is accused of.
“If he was, the Reform leader must explain why he thought it was appropriate for Madgwick to stand for his party, hold a local leadership role, and to work as a Reform member of staff.”

Madgwick began his political career as an independent on Portsmouth city council, winning his seat in 2021. In 2025, he joined Reform UK, and a year later he became a Hampshire councillor, representing the North East Havant area.

He was one of 20 Reform councillors to be elected, placing them third behind the Conservatives, who run the authority, and the Liberal Democrats. Madgwick became leader of the Reform group, and chair of the council’s corporate services and resources select committee.

In September, when masked protesters connected to the far right activist Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, blocked roads in Portsmouth over the arrival of asylum seekers on small boats, Madgwick was at the scene and spoke to the media.

While saying it was important any protests were peaceful, Madgwick said local people were “not happy, and rightly so” about the arrival of asylum seekers. He was involved recently in an incident in which protesters gathered outside a Portsmouth hotel after mistaking Pakistan’s under-19s cricket team for asylum seekers, liaising with hotel staff and persuading protesters to leave.

Madgwick called the hotel to mediate between staff and the assembled crowd, and said at the time that it was a “massively unfortunate incident”. He added, however, that he believed the incident was understandable given recent coverage of asylum seekers arriving in the city via small boats.

Madgwick later posted on X: “I am shocked and dismayed at the charges brought against me. Whilst the charges are extremely serious, I will say unequivocally that I am innocent of the allegations against me. Due process must take its course and the legal process must be followed without hindrance.

“I considered it responsible to resign as Reform UK leader in Hampshire Council and I will continue as an independent until I’m cleared. I will not make any further statement now, or in the future, on this in any capacity. I will deactivate my social media shortly until due process has concluded.”
