articles.title: NTSB says crucial plane parts found three miles from Florida crash site
articles.summary: The NTSB said because the parts were found far from the accident site, they fell off before the crash.

blocks.text: "Knowing that it was lost is a very important piece of evidence in terms of pointing us towards other things to investigate," he said.
Chapman said officials were still working out whether losing the left elevator caused the plane to nosedive or whether the part fell off because "forces on the aircraft caused that to separate".
He said the part of the plane that controls upward and downward movement may not have been "effective" at the speed the plane was travelling.
The Learjet 60 was bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas, when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway and exploded on impact.
In air traffic control audio recordings, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and that the crew was "managing the ice".
They are then heard saying the plane was "picking up precipitation" and "we need to climb". Moments later, the same voice said the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.
An emergency was declared and the pilots can be heard yelling "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".
NTSB plans to investigate the role weather played in the crash. Officials were struggling to access the wreckage due to the huge crater created by the jet on a road in Palm Beach.
Chapman said on Tuesday that the force of the impact severely damaged the wreckage.

Seven passengers died on board, named in a joint statement as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife, Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - as well as friends of the family Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and Anita Maria Cetina, a nanny.
The pilot was named in media reports as 55-year-old Jeffrey Gregory. Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the co-pilot.

articles.title: Spanish transport minister resigns after deadly train crash
articles.summary:
Óscar Puente also announces his withdrawal from upcoming election following disaster that killed 69 people

Spain’s transport minister handed in his resignation on Tuesday after the train…

blocks.text: Spain’s transport minister handed in his resignation on Tuesday after the train crash that killed 69 people last week, one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century.

Óscar Puente, who had earlier pledged to work “tirelessly” to restore confidence in the world’s second-largest high-speed rail network, also said he was withdrawing from the country’s upcoming general election.

Last week’s crash, and another disaster earlier this year, have overshadowed campaigning for the 29 November ballot, in which the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, is trailing in opinion polls.
Puente had ruled out resigning on several occasions since the disaster.

But at the end of a lengthy hearing before lawmakers, he said: “I wish to inform you that I am not only stepping down from my position as minister of transport, but that I am also withdrawing my name from the lists for the early legislative elections on 29 November.”

Hours earlier, at a press conference during which he presented measures to improve safety, the minister had said the government would “work tirelessly to achieve and regain the public’s trust in high-speed rail”.
The rightwing opposition, which had demanded Puente’s resignation, and unions had criticised him for appearing to pin all the blame for the disaster on one control centre operator.

The crash happened when a train operated by the state-owned company Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to the private Spanish operator Iryo on Wednesday outside the village of Urda, about 80 miles south of Madrid.

blocks.caption: Work on clearing the wreckage of the crash in Toledo has continued this week. Photograph: Angeles Visdomine/EPA

blocks.text: The failure of an automatic safety system halted all trains on a 39-mile stretch of track, but a control centre nonetheless authorised the Renfe service to resume its journey.

Among the measures announced at the earlier press conference by Puente was the creation of software for control centres that would issue automatic alerts and make it easier to spot anomalies in traffic.
Puente said an AI agent would be created to oversee the system and “minimise the possibility of human error”, describing the proposal as unprecedented.
In scenarios where a control centre operator took a decision while the automatic safety system was down, a second operator would have to confirm it, Puente added.
after newsletter promotion
The train drivers’ union Semaf, which has called strikes at Renfe for 10 and 12 November, has denounced a worsening of working conditions and the use of “degraded systems”.

Critics say investment in maintenance has not kept up with the increase in passenger numbers since the 2021 liberalisation of Spain’s rail network, which allowed private companies to break Renfe’s decades-long monopoly.
In an apparent recognition of the unions’ demands, Puente said the working conditions of control centre operators would be reformed, including their breaks and by monitoring their fatigue levels.
Puente also announced an aid package of €30m (£25m) for the families of the dead and the scores of people who were injured in the crash.

Another collision in the southern region of Andalusia in January killed 46 people on the same key line connecting Madrid with the city of Seville, Spain’s first high-speed route when it opened in 1992.

articles.title: How a First Nation is pushing back against Canada's largest AI data centre
articles.summary: Construction is well underway for what is set to be Canada’s largest data centre, located just outside Regina. Some Saskatchewan First Nations are pushing back, saying there will be major effects to…

image.caption: Meleah Isnana, left, and her great grandmother Dianne Goodwill, right, stand behind Echo Lake. They say Standing Buffalo Dakota First Nation is trying to protect lakes like this from potential pollution from Canada's largest data centre, which is being built an hour's drive away. (Halyna Mihalik/CBC

blocks.text: Dianne Goodwill and her great-granddaughter look out at the lakes surrounding their First Nation, breathing in the air on a warm autumn day.

The 73-year-old elder doesn't take the clean air and water for granted. She and others from Standing Buffalo Dakota First Nation say Bell Canada's construction of the Canada’s largest AI data centre has sparked concern about potential water, air and light pollution.
“It’s not exactly here, but it's within miles,” Goodwill said. “It's not [a] good idea to have something that big around our area.”
The data centre is being built in the RM of Sherwood just outside of Regina, about an hour’s drive from Standing Buffalo.
“We need to stand and speak on those important things because it is for the benefit of the future of our children,” Goodwill said.
Her 14-year-old great granddaughter said the school in Standing Buffalo has been trying to prevent the use of AI.
“It's quite harmful [be]cause what AI can do is dangerous," said Meleah Isnana, who’s in Grade 9. "Like photoshopping, making different photos and using AI to spread misinformation.”

People fishing at Pasqua Lake in Standing Buffalo Dakota First Nation in October. Chief Rodger Redman says he's concerned the water may be polluted by Canada's largest AI data centre. (Will Draper/CBC)

Standing Buffalo Chief Rodger Redman has been advocating against the data centre. He said he wants to protect the traditional land he grew up on from potential pollution once the facility is up and running.
“We have to live here, live in this toxic waste that’s going to be left,” Redman said.
“Anything that has that living spirit, we have to safeguard that, because whatever happens to them is going [to] happen to us.”

Redman formally raised his concerns with Bell on Oct. 2, requesting the scientific studies, regulatory approvals and environmental information necessary to examine the project’s impacts on what he said is Standing Buffalo’s unceded traditional territory.
The First Nation is one of few in the province not under a formal treaty, but is protected under the Indian Act.
Redman said he’s prepared to take Bell Canada to court if current environmental assessments aren’t shared, with a plan to pursue a moratorium on the project.
“Work with us, give us these answers, let us do our own assessments, recognize the rights of the Indian people,” Redman said.
“We’re the narrative of our own legislation.”
Chief Rodger Redman of Standing Buffalo Dakota First Nation looks out into the land he grew up on. (Will Draper/CBC)

Bell Canada declined an interview with CBC, but said in a statement that it has offered to meet with the First Nation and Standing Buffalo has yet to take the company up on the offer. Bell Canada said an environmental assessment will be made public with the project’s next expansion phase.
The $52-billion facility stands as Canada's largest single private sector capital investment.
Bell Canada told CBC that “protecting the land, water and the people who live nearby has guided the design of this campus from the start.”
The company pointed to a sealed, closed-loop water cooling system to minimize waste. It said the system can run for more than 10 years without the fluid needing to be changed or topped up.
First Nations demand Bell release environmental assessment of new AI data centre
Bell Canada also said it is working with First Nations in Saskatchewan.
The George Gordon First Nation Development Corporation partnered with Bell on the project and said it is opening up work for Indigenous people in a new sector.
“These projects are going to happen,” said Don Ross, the company’s CEO. “So we can either be in front of them or we can sit across the street and complain about them being built.”
George Gordon First Nation owns land that borders the site. Ross said about 85 Indigenous people have already been hired to help build the data centre.
“We want to be employed and trained and have careers just like the rest of Saskatchewan people,” he said. “That’s what we’re doing with Bell.”
Don Ross is the CEO of George Gordon Developments. He says the data centre has already hired about 85 Indigenous workers (Halyna Mihalik/CBC)

Ross said he’d like to see an HR plan from Bell to confirm how many Indigenous people it will commit to hiring once the centre is running, so that he can begin helping people with relevant degrees ready themselves for the jobs.

Bell Canada told CBC that once the centre is running it will create 280 to 500 permanent roles between the data centres and power generation, along with up to 100 management roles at a new Bell AI Fabric head office in Regina.
Ross said environmental oversight between the First Nation and Bell was a part of their agreement.
He noted that a hum can be heard from the site, but said mitigation measures like berms are in place to address that issue.
Widespread pushback, protests
Opposition to the data centre extends beyond Standing Buffalo Dakota First Nation.
There have been multiple protests against it this year in Saskatchewan. People say there’s been a lack of transparency on environmental protocol and no public consultation for those living nearby.

“That's one thing that I'm worried about for this data centre, if they're going to keep diesel on site and what plans they're going to have in place if something should occur,” protester Dylan Block said at a rally at the RM of Sherwood’s office in late October.
“If you're keeping diesel on site, there is no way to guarantee that it will not leak.”
Dylan Block, left, says he has attended five rallies against the creation of the data centre this year. (Halyna Mihalik/CBC)
Block said he agrees with Standing Buffalo’s requests for the environmental assessments to be made public.
“This is their land and it seems that Bell data centre is not interested in respecting that,” he said.
Breaking into the data sector

In June the federal government launched its AI for All strategy, aiming to secure Canadian data assets and reduce reliance on foreign tech providers. Massive data centres are popping up across the country, from Alberta to Nova Scotia, and now the 1.2-gigawatt project in Saskatchewan.
Business analyst Keith Willoughby said the centre is new ground for the province.
“We in Saskatchewan have been a resource driven economy for decades,” said Willoughby, the dean of the Edwards School of Business at the University of Saskatchewan.
“The data centre, however, allows us the ability to participate in the intellectual economy, in the tech sector, in a deeper way.”
The footprint of an AI data centre under construction in Regina, Saskatchewan. (Adam Bent/CBC)
The provincial government has worked to support Bell on the project and said the development will greatly benefit Saskatchewan’s economy.
“There's literally hundreds of people working out there today,” Saskatchewan’s Crown Investments Corporation Minister Jeremy Harrison said.

“[It’s] one of the largest construction sites in the entire country right now, which is going to generate enormous opportunities as far as jobs, as far as the economy, not just here in Regina, but right across the entire province.”
Standing Buffalo tells CBC it will continue to seek the underlying provincial determination, scientific studies and regulatory records necessary to independently examine the data centre.
Two data halls are expected to be up and running in the first half of 2027.

articles.title: Spanish transport minister resigns days after deadly train crash
articles.summary: At least 69 people were killed and dozens injured in the collision south of the capital, Madrid.

blocks.text: Puente announced his decision at the end of a congressional session on Tuesday evening in which he had outlined new rail safety measures and been grilled by the opposition.
He said he had taken the decision to resign immediately after the 28 October disaster, but had not made it public.
Puente had been under mounting pressure in the wake of the disaster as opposition parties and some allies of the government called on him to step down.
His resignation comes as a blow to the Socialist-led government ahead of a general election set for 29 November.

During his lengthy hearing before lawmakers, Puente said: "I wish to inform you that I am not only stepping down from my position as minister of transport, but that I am also withdrawing my name from the lists for the early legislative elections."
Leaked audio recordings published in Spanish media soon after the crash revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the disaster.

The three recordings of conversations between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stopped on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said that authorities will "get to the bottom of every last detail of this tragedy".
Last week's crash was one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013. The country observed three days of mourning after the tragedy.
The moving train, run by state-owned operator Renfe, had 397 passengers on board. The stationary train was run by private operator Iryo, and carrying 147 passengers.
A reported issue with the automatic signalling system - a computer failure - had forced all trains to halt on the affected stretch.
But later the Renfe train was ordered to proceed in "error", according to Puente.
The audio recordings were published by several Spanish news outlets including El Pais and RTVE.
In one, a control centre operator is speaking to the driver of the Renfe train, which was having some technical difficulties.
After some exchanges, the control operator tells the driver: "Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation."
The driver replies: "At normal speed?" To which the controller answers: "Yes."
The Lateral Signalling Block is a back-up or alternative train system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.
The driver of the stationary Iryo train says in another audio recording that communication with the train-control system has been lost, and it is not moving.
The train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda", the driver tells the control centre operator. After a series of exchanges, the driver is then told to "resume the journey" normally.

The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.
The latter recording suggests that the controller had been notified that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached.
Iryo said its carriages were "struck from behind" by the other train.
Puente said last week that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".

articles.title: King Charles addresses summit as demands for slavery apology grow
articles.summary:
Speaking in Antigua, the king did not give explicit support for reparations but said he wanted to ‘address past wrongs’

King Charles has said that deepening his understanding of the horrors…

blocks.text: King Charles has said that deepening his understanding of the horrors of slavery has made him more determined to address the wrongs of the past, as Caribbean leaders and campaigners intensified demands for an apology and reparations from Britain.
“We cannot change the actions of those who came before us,” Charles told leaders at the opening of the Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda on Tuesday. “We can, however, learn from the past.

“The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth,” he said. “That shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow.”
Charles said the more he had furthered his understanding “through listening, learning and looking”, the more committed he had become to building modern partnerships capable of addressing past wrongs.

But the king stopped short of an apology or explicit support for reparations, instead pointing to education, employment, intra-Commonwealth trade and climate resilience as ways of tackling continuing hardship and disadvantage.
“For, as any sailor navigating the seas knows, we cannot command the winds, least of all where the winds of yesterday have delivered us, but we can choose how we set our sail,” he said.

Though speaking as head of the Commonwealth, and this speech would have been drafted by Charles personally along with his advisers, palace aides have indicated there would be “no surprises” in it for the UK government.
Andy Burnham refused to be drawn on whether the UK might offer further financial contributions to the Commonwealth stopping short of direct reparations.
The UK prime minister told reporters: “I’ve been very clear that we do not support reparations, and I made that quite abundantly clear in the piece that I wrote in advance of coming here.

“But it’s not the case that we don’t support countries in the Commonwealth around development and helping them with debt issues that they’ve got, green finance. That’s what we’ve done under all governments, and in my view, we should continue to do as part of being a Commonwealth.”

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham walks to meet members of the waiting media on the sidelines of the summit at the American University of Antigua in Osbourn. Photograph: Kin Cheung/Reuters

blocks.text: Pressed on whether this could mean additional financial contributions that would weigh on the taxpayer, Burnham said: “Well, you’re getting ahead. What we need to have is that meaningful dialogue where we take time to listen, and let’s be clear: the Commonwealth is an important part of our trade too.

“It’s a two-way arrangement. You know, trade is up between the UK and the rest of the Commonwealth in the last year quite significantly, actually. So you need to see it in that way as well. It benefits Britain to be here, listening to people, building that new partnership, and that’s good for growth in Britain.”

Reparations are not formally on the agenda of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm), where trade, climate resilience and finance, sustainable debt, democracy and opportunities for young people were among the stated priorities of the 56-member bloc.
But sustained campaigning by Caribbean governments and a growing international reparations movement have propelled the issue to the centre of political debate surrounding the gathering.

Opening the summit in St John’s, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda, the country’s prime minister, Gaston Browne, said “fairness” required an “honest engagement with our shared history” and called for meaningful and respectful dialogue on reparatory justice and the enduring consequences of slavery and colonialism.

blocks.caption: King Charles III speaks with students during the Commonwealth Youth Forum at the University of West Indies in St John’s, Antigua. Photograph: Chris Jackson/PA

blocks.text: Burnham had said he was open to Britain apologising for slavery, with officials holding talks with national leaders in Antigua about what that could entail.
He has also proposed discussions on debt resets for smaller Commonwealth nations and announced £40m ($54m) for critical infrastructure in the Caribbean over the next three years.

But Caribbean leaders have stressed that dialogue must extend beyond an apology. Philip J Pierre, the chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom), described an apology as an “essential first step” but said an “apology without repair is incomplete”.

He said any structured dialogue must allow consideration of the entirety of Caricom’s 10-point reparations plan, including public health, education, cultural restitution, psychological rehabilitation, debt cancellation and monetary compensation.

Britain’s royal family benefited from the trade, but Charles is politically neutral and is not expected to offer an apology. A palace spokesperson said it would “not be appropriate” for the king to announce a change in government policy.

According to the AFP news agency, Burnham discussed slavery with the Barbados prime minister, Mia Mottley, during a meeting on Monday, one of several bilateral meetings the prime minister is expected to have at the summit.
They discussed how Britain was “offering a structured dialogue for communities impacted by the transatlantic slave trade”, including the “next steps”, Downing Street said.

blocks.caption: Burnham is said to have discussed the impact of slavery with Mia Mottley during talks on Monday. Photograph: Kin Cheung/PA

blocks.text: Outside the heavily secured summit venue, protesters gathered with placards declaring: “We know what you did and we can see you,” and “You say appalling atrocity, yet you refuse to apologise.”

One protester, Lenworth Johnson, said that if the king’s constitutional position prevented him from apologising, the British government should authorise him to do so. “We feel an apology is necessary,” he said.

Another, Radcliffe Robins, said the wealth enjoyed by Britain and other western powers was built in part on enslavement. “It is absolutely necessary that his majesty the king and the royal family apologise for the brutality and the injustice that they have imposed on us,” he said. “And with that, we ask for reparations.”
Another protester said the demonstration was intended to ensure those entering the summit knew campaigners were “watching them and listening to what they’re saying and what they’re doing”.

Dorbrene O’Marde, chair of the Antigua and Barbuda Reparations Support Commission and one of the organisers, said: “One whose heart is filled with horror and whose soul bears the most profound personal sorrow must surely be moved beyond words – beyond repeated emotional expression without acceptance of responsibility.

“Genuine moral consciousness demands apologies – the acknowledgment of wrong, the acceptance of responsibility and the commitment to pursue reparations. Unfortunately King Charles III does nothing of the sort. He has again failed the people who recognise him as king.”
The demonstrations followed a reparations event on Monday hosted by the House of Commons’ all-party parliamentary group for Afrikan Reparations alongside campaign organisations.

blocks.caption: Delegates attend an opening ceremony for the summit on Tuesday. Photograph: Canadian Press/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Its chair, the Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, welcomed debt relief but warned against presenting it as reparations.

“Reparations was never about personal guilt. It is about the responsibility of states and institutions that still stand,” she said. “Aid is not reparations, because aid leaves the power with the giver. Agency was the crime. Agency has to be the remedy.”

The meeting was followed by a candlelight vigil on an Antiguan beach commemorating enslaved Africans brought to the island. The Rev Bonnie Smith, president of the Antigua Christian Council, asked those gathered to remember people torn from their homes, separated from their families and forced across the Atlantic into enslavement.
“Their names may be absent from our records, but they are not absent from your love,” she said. “Their voices may have been silenced, but their lives have never ceased to matter.”
Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, chair of the Caricom Reparations Commission, meanwhile framed the campaign as part of a wider struggle for peace and justice.
“We are concerned about the unleashing of terror and violence upon innocent people,” he said.
“We believe that reparatory justice that calls for human decency, equality and justice for all is the philosophy that will hold us together as humanity going into this 21st century.”

Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the Repair Campaign, the reparatory justice movement, said he believed Charles’s expressions of sorrow over slavery were sincere, but was disappointed he had not gone any further than his previous remarks.
“The apology hasn’t come. And there’s no talk about reparatory justice. So to that extent, this speech to me was a disappointment,” he said.
The king’s reference to support for health, education and infrastructure, Gonsalves said, concerned subjects already covered in the agreements in the UN sustainable development goals.
“What we are saying is that there has to be, additionally … a special carve-out in respect of reparatory justice,” he added.

articles.title: Spain transport minister offers resignation in wake of train accident
articles.summary: After two deadly train crashes this year, Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente has said he will step down.

image.caption: Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente had requested a parliamentary committee convene TuesdayImage: Diego Radamés/Europa Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente offered his resignation on Tuesday in the wake of one of Europe's worst rail disasters in recent memory last week that killed 69 people.

The tragedy, Spain's second fatal rail collision in less than a year, has intensified scrutiny of railway safety and added political pressure on Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez ahead of parliamentary elections on November 29.
In January, a train crash in the southern Andalusia region killed 46 people.
"A transport ​minister ‌in a country like Spain cannot continue in ‌office with two accidents ‌of ​this severity in less than a year," he told lawmakers while announcing his intention to resign.
Puente, member of Sanchez's Spanish Socialist Workers' Party, also said he would withdraw his name from the list of parliamentary electioncandidates. He did not specify when he would leave ​his post.
Puente's political opponents had demanded he step down, while train unions had been unhappy with him for appearing to pin blame for the disaster on one rail control center operator.
Second rail accident in a year kills dozens in central Spain
Government unveils new rail safety measures

Just hours before addressing lawmakers, Puente had presented improved rail network safety measures and told a press conference the government would "work tirelessly to achieve and regain the public's trust in high-speed rail."

This included plans for control center software that would issue automatic alerts and make it easier to spot traffic anomalies, and an AI agent for system oversight to "minimize the possibility of human error."
Another measure Puente mentioned was requiring a second operator confirm decisions made in scenarios involving a faulty automatic safety system.
The accident happened during the failure of an automated safety system that had stopped all trains along a 63-kilometer stretch of track between Madrid and Seville on Wednesday morning.
Despite the stoppage on the line, a control center allowed a high-speed train operated by state-owned rail company Renfe to continue its journey.
The Renfe train collided with stopped train owned by private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda in Toledo province.
Spain rail crash piles pressure on government before vote

articles.title: Two Australians confirmed dead in Spain’s high-speed train crash
articles.summary:
Legal body handling identification says three latest victims include two Australians and a Japanese citizen

  • Get our

blocks.text: Two Australians are among 69 people who died in last week’s high-speed train collision after Spanish authorities confirmed the identities of three more victims.

A legal body set up to handle the identification work, made up of police and forensics experts, announced in a statement late on Monday the three latest confirmed victims – two Australians and a Japanese citizen. They have not been named.
In a statement on Wednesday morning, Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade confirmed it was providing consular assistance to the families of two Australians who had died.
“We send our deepest condolences to the families at this difficult time.”

The Spanish centre for data integration released the following statement on social media: “The families of the 69 individuals have been notified as well as the relevant consular offices in the case of deceased foreign nationals.”

On Tuesday evening the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said she sent her “deepest condolences on behalf of Australia” to her Spanish counterpart, José Manuel Albares, and to the people of Spain following the “devastating” train collision.
“Our thoughts are with those who have lost loved ones, those injured and all affected by this tragedy.”

Wednesday’s disaster – one of Europe’s deadliest rail accidents this century – has resulted in victims’ relatives enduring an agonising wait as forensics teams identify the dead, sometimes from individual body parts.
Spain’s transport minister, Oscar Puente, has announced his resignation over the fatal crash.
It’s the European country’s second train accident this year.
“A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot continue in office with two accidents of this severity in less than a year,” he told a parliamentary committee.

blocks.caption: The accident was Spain’s second high-speed train collision this year. Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The victims include 54 Spanish nationals and 15 foreigners – four US citizens, two Australians, two Japanese and one each from Argentina, Canada, France, Mexico, Portugal, Tunisia and the Czech Republic.
On Friday, Dfat confirmed it was providing consular assistance to the family of two Australians in connection with the crash.

The accident was Spain’s second high-speed train collision this year and raised fresh questions about the country’s rail safety, after a crash in the southern region of Andalusia in January killed 46 people.

The latest disaster struck when a service by state operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to Spanish company Iryo outside the central village of Urda, about 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The failure of an automatic safety system halted all trains on a 63km stretch of track, but a control centre authorised the Renfe service to resume its journey while the other train was still.
Labor MP Jason Clare said on Thursday accidents of this kind were “something people never, ever recover from”.
“The whole country is in shock at the moment, seeing these images on our screens. It’s just horrific,” he told ABC TV.

articles.title: Correction on our previous reporting on charges faced by Alberta hockey executive
articles.summary: CBC News received information from the courts that was inaccurate.

blocks.text: Calgary
CBC News received information from the courts that was inaccurate.
Incorrect information provided by court
On Nov. 3, 2026, CBC News reported that a former Alberta hockey executive facing child luring charges was also wanted on warrants for domestic violence.
That reporting was incorrect.
CBC News received information from the courts that was inaccurate after the Alberta Court of Justice merged the files of two different men so they appeared in court records as one.

Tyler Robb King, 39, was arrested Friday and charged with luring, sexual exploitation and making child sexual abuse material. The offences are alleged to have taken place between 2021 and 2024 when King worked for the Okotoks Oilers of the British Columbia Hockey League as assistant general manager of operations.

articles.title: Greenland's parliament ratifies Trump's US security agreement
articles.summary: The US is set to expand its military footprint on the Arctic island, part of the Kingdom of Denmark. It follows pressure from Donald Trump earlier in the year which opened a major rift in the…

image.caption: The Pituffik Space Base is the last remaining US base on Greenland [FILE: Oct 4, 2023]Image: Thomas Traasdahl/Ritzau Scanpix/AP

blocks.text: Greenland's parliament on Tuesday signed off on a trilateral security and military-access agreement with the United States and Denmark that paves the way for an expanded US' military presence on the strategically located and mineral-rich island.

The deal has alleviated pressure coming from US President Donald Trump, who earlier this year had repeatedly threatened to take control of the self-governing Danish territory, citing US security interests.

After months of negotiation the agreement was signed in September by Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

The agreement allows for two new US military bases and Trump's "Golden Dome" missile defence system. It also keeps Greenland under Danish control, while reaffirming Greenlanders' right to self determination.
Greenland cannot take 'stability for granted'
On Tuesday, shortly before the vote in the capital, Nuuk, Greenlandic Foreign Minister Mute Egede welcomed the agreement's ratification.
"We must accept that peace and stability are no longer something we can take for granted," Egede said.
In a first debate last month, a majority of Greenlandic lawmakers had already signalled support for the agreement.
Pele Broberg, chair of the pro-independence Naleraq party, questioned the deal's value for Greenland.
"We are looking for a better agreement that we can benefit from when we become an independent state. But no economic benefit has been gained from the agreement," Broberg said.
The agreement will come into effect after ratification by the Danish parliament, which is due to read the bill over two sessions in November. A vote is scheduled for November 19 in Copenhagen.
What's really in the Greenland deal?
Trump pressures Greenland
In January 2026, Trump began calling for the US to control Greenland, and threatened the use of military force and tariffs against US European allies if he did not get his way.
Trump had claimed that Denmark was not doing enough to defend its autonomous arctic territory from unspecified threats from China and Russia.
Trump's repeated threats damaged US ties with Denmark and rattled the US' European NATO allies.

On January 21, after Trump met with NATO chief Mark Rutte on the sidelines of the Global Economic Forum in Davos, tensions cooled after Rutte and Trump announced the "concept of a deal" allowing for expanded US defense access to Greenland, which would later evolve into the agreement signed in September.
Denmark had repeatedly said it was willing to discuss expanding the US military footprint in Greenland, while rejecting Trump's more extreme demand that Greenland become US territory.
Critics have pointed out the same deal could have been made without the extreme disruption caused by Trump's territorial and tariff threats.

Under a 1951 agreement, the US already has considerable military freedom of action in Greenland. After years of voluntarily drawing down its military presence, only the Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland remains, which is used for missile defense and radar surveillance.
What did Trump really gain from the Greenland deal?

articles.title: Alberta to lawyer up if NDP challenges electoral boundary report: Smith
articles.summary: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said Tuesday her government will assemble a legal team to make the argument that new electoral boundaries proposed by an advisory panel achieve effective…

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said so-called hybrid ridings like those being proposed in Lethbridge are accepted practice and work elsewhere in the province. (Manuel Carrillos-Avalos/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Calgary·New

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said Tuesday her government will assemble a legal team to make the argument that new electoral boundaries proposed by an advisory panel achieve effective representation, should the Opposition NDP advance a legal challenge.
Report issued Monday proposes shifting thousands of Calgary, Lethbridge voters into rural-urban districts

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said her government will assemble a legal team to make the case that new proposed electoral boundaries achieve effective representation, if the Opposition NDP advances a legal challenge.
"I hope it doesn't come to that. I hope we'll be able to have a debate in the legislature," Smith told reporters at the Rural Municipalities of Alberta convention on Tuesday.
On Monday, an advisory panel issued a report on Alberta’s electoral boundaries.
It proposed, among other changes, expanding a few Calgary ridings across municipal boundaries, and establishing a sole urban seat for Lethbridge plus three hybrid urban-rural seats.
Provincial boundary adjustments, made every eight to 10 years, are typically not fare for intrigue.

Not so when it came to this round, which involved a long road with many twists, like the rejection of a prior commission's proposals and Alberta's acting chief justice characterizing the process as "irregular."

items: Boundary commission chair questions motives of UCP-picked panellists in final riding report
Alberta’s acting chief justice won’t ask judges to chair new electoral boundaries panel

blocks.text: The Alberta NDP has said that it will take the new maps to court on constitutional grounds. On Monday, Opposition Leader Naheed Nenshi specifically highlighted the Lethbridge proposal.
"I believe that this report is illegal. I believe it is unconstitutional," Nenshi said.
The resulting electoral boundaries brew contains the distinctive sour odour of partisanship.Keith Archer, served on a previous Alberta commission
Brian O’Ferrall, the retired Alberta Court of Appeal justice that headed up the panel, wrote in an executive summary that he did not believe that the proposals were unconstitutional.

The minority of the panel — Gerard Kennedy, a professor of constitutional law at the University of Alberta, as well as Brent Robinson, who was a councillor for the town of Okotoks — disagreed, writing that they expected the courts would get involved.
Lethbridge 'well-served' by hybrid ridings: Smith
Effective representation is the legal principle that allows for the balancing of equal-sized voter populations with other factors, like geography.
Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Smith said Lethbridge would be "very well-served" by having four representatives.
She added that she currently represents a hybrid riding, in Brooks-Medicine Hat.
"Hybrid ridings ... may not make sense in all circumstances, but they certainly do in some," Smith said, adding that she would be briefed on the full report later on Tuesday.
Currently, Lethbridge is divided into two ridings within city limits: Lethbridge-East and Lethbridge-West.
The majority of the panel suggested sketching three ruralized ridings that stretch far from Lethbridge in all directions

items: Lethbridge-Cardston, which would go about 100 kilometres southwest to Waterton Lakes National Park and the U.S. border.
Lethbridge-Taber-Warner, which would stretch east about 140 kilometres to the rural area directly south of Medicine Hat.
Lethbridge-Little Bow, which would extend north about 140 kilometres to Highway 1 near Strathmore.

blocks.text: A map showing a sole Lethbridge urban seat, as well as three hybrid electoral divisions combining parts of the city with vast surrounding rural regions. (Advisory panel on electoral boundaries)

The majority of the panel argued that southern Alberta was "uniquely united" economically around the agricultural and food processing industries, while the minority wrote they found that suggestion "highly questionable," suggesting it reduced effective representation.

Keith Archer, who served on a previous Alberta commission and was chief electoral officer in British Columbia, wrote in an email that he was not supportive of the process that had played out over the past several months.

"The resulting electoral boundaries brew contains the distinctive sour odour of partisanship in which the government replaces an administrative review of electoral boundaries with a highly political review. Albertans are not well-served by this process," he wrote.
Alberta’s history with these commissions has typically seen the recommendations turned into law.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Joel is a reporter/editor with CBC Calgary. In fall 2021, he spent time with CBC's bureau in Lethbridge. He was previously the editor of the Airdrie City View and Rocky View Weekly newspapers. He hails from Swift Current, Sask. Reach him by email at joel.dryden@cbc.ca

articles.title: Home in Amherstburg, Ont., unlivable after family spent $155K on renovations, police looking for contractor
articles.summary: Tonya Azevedo says she lost $155,000 and her family of four can no longer live in their home of 20 years after a contractor who told them he was licensed did work that turned out to be unsafe. “I’m…

image.caption: Amherstburg, Ont., resident Tonya Azevedo stands in the backyard of her Alma Street home that her family can't live in because of unsafe work done during renovations. (Jason Viau/CBC)

blocks.text: Windsor

Tonya Azevedo says she lost $155,000 and her family of four can no longer live in their home of 20 years after a contractor who told them he was licensed did work that turned out to be unsafe. “I’m absolutely heartbroken,” says Azevedo, who had remortgaged her home to pay for the renos.
'This is just the level of destruction that we’re left with,' says Tonya Azevedo
Tonya Azevedo says she has lost $155,000 and her family of four can no longer live in their home of 20 years after a contractor who told them he was licensed did work that turned out to be unsafe.
Azevedo said she discovered dirt used to fill concrete blocks in the foundation of the home’s addition, live electrical wiring under drywall and a sewer pipe that was ruptured.
The Town of Amherstburg even ordered a stop to construction because the work didn’t match approved drawings and “multiple deficiencies” were found, according to documents obtained by CBC News.
“I’m absolutely heartbroken,” said Azevedo. “Every time I come here and see what’s left of a home that I raised my two children in and all of the happy memories … it’s just gone.”
She remortgaged her Alma Street home to get $200,000 from the bank for an addition and new garage.
There were plans to build onto the rear of the home, expand the family kitchen and the master bedroom, and add an en suite bathroom and a third bedroom upstairs.
Azevedo said she just finished spending the remainder of the loan undoing and fixing the contractor's work.
In the meantime, the family is living with a relative. Azevedo and her husband are sleeping in that home's laundry room.
“We don’t have a home,” said Azevedo. “This is just the level of destruction that we’re left with.”
Police looking to charge contractor
Windsor police said Tuesday that there's now a warrant out for the arrest of contractor Jessie Flaricee after Azevedo filed a report with Windsor police's Amherstburg detachment.
Flaricee is wanted on fraud over $5,000, uttering a forged document and obtaining more than $5,000 under false pretenses.
His company, MBS Home Solutions, was dissolved for non-compliance in November 2024, according to Windsor police.
During a conversation with CBC News on Monday, Flaricee said he offered to fix the issues, has made attempts to reach out to the family and there’s been a communication breakdown.
“They pretty much fired me and didn’t give me the opportunity to fix any issues."
Jessie Flaricee is the owner of MBS Building Solutions and did work on Azevedo's home from March to August. (Facebook)
Flaricee said he also hired subcontractors, but didn’t specify who did the problematic work.

“There is more to the story than portraying it as a contractor trying to take somebody’s money. That’s not even close to the case,” said Flaricee. “There are a lot of layers to this situation that are far more complex than what is being portrayed.”
When asked if there's any remaining money that could be returned to Azevedo, Flaricee said “that’ll be between me and her.”
“There’s no intent to take anything from anybody,” said Flaricee.
Azevedo said Flaricee told her he was a fully licensed contractor, something she says is not true.
“I guess it expired, so I had to renew it, but I’m insured. My bank account is under my business name and my name,” he said.
“People have now touched that project and started working and undoing or doing [work]."
'We trusted this person'
Azevedo said her husband knew Flaricee from the local youth football community and he quickly became a family friend.
“We trusted this person,” said Azevedo. “Maybe we shouldn’t have listened to him and had just done some more research. I was just too trusting of him.”
The Better Business Bureau (BBB) said every contractor should provide the type of licence they have, what agency it’s registered with and when it expires.

“So if you want to dig into the broader term of validating licensing, check directly with the issuing authority, which is easy to do online as well,” said Jennifer Matthews, CEO of the BBB in southwestern Ontario.
Some tips for consumer protection
Matthews said people should also ask for three references.
The BBB’s website allows the public to check the experience and reputation of companies, which Matthews also recommends doing.
“You can look at are their complaints against that business, how have they been resolved."

Demolition and construction first began in March, when she first gave Flaricee $45,000 to get started. That’s when the family packed up all of their things and moved out while the work was being done.
They moved back in by June and then the work stopped in August.
Azevedo said Flaricee asked for more money, but she refused.
She remembers telling him that she doesn’t “feel comfortable giving you any more money until there is close to $155,000 worth of work here and a home that we can live in safely.”
Tonya Azevedo, left, is seen with her husband, Joel Charron, right, her son, Bradley Azevedo and her daughter, Jocelyn Azevedo. (Tonya Azevedo)
In Azevedo's case, there was an attempt to figure out where the money went. She said she asked for invoices and receipts, and never received them.
But Flaricee insisted he was fired and not given the opportunity to fix the problems.
Son's 'safe space and sanctuary' is now gone
Either way, Azevedo said, there’s been a lot of “stress and trauma” put on her family throughout this process.
Her 16-year-old son, who has autism, just wants his bedroom back. She calls it his “safe space and sanctuary" and said it's taken a toll on his mental health.
“To have everything stripped away from them and as a mom, not being able to fix that," said Azevedo.
The town’s building department noted that the foundation mortar joints didn’t comply with the Ontario Building Code and new part of the foundation was not connected to the existing foundation.
After the contractor’s demolition, Azevedo said, there’s been no heat in the home, the family is without a washroom and there isn’t power to much of the house.
“We’re not asking for our home to be finished. We’re just asking for our home back."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jason Viau is reporter for CBC News based in Windsor, Ont. He has an interest in telling stories related to accountability, policing, court, crime and municipal affairs. You can email story ideas and tips to jason.viau@cbc.ca.

articles.title: UK's King Charles III decries 'monstrous injustice' of slave trade
articles.summary: King Charles has told leaders at a Commonwealth summit that the legacy of the transatlantic slave trade "fills my heart with horror." He did not address calls for apologies and reparations.

image.caption: King Charles III opened the 28th Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting with earnest words of reflection, though he offered no apologies for the British Empire's role in the transatlantic slave tradeImage: Ben Stansall/REUTERS

blocks.text: The United Kingdom's King Charles III on Tuesday opened this week's Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, a summit of 56 Commonwealth member-state leaders, by speaking of the tragic legacy of the transatlantic slave trade.
Charles told those gathered that he had furthered his "own understanding of the issues through listening, learning and looking."

"The ​transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth. As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with ⁠horror ​and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."

The monarch stopped short of apologizing for Britain's role in the dark trade, as well as refraining from any talk of reparations. Instead, he spoke of the need to look forward when addressing the "monstrous injustice" of the past to insure that "evil need not have the last word."
Ghana revives slave trade history through theater
Will the UK apologize for slavery, offer reparations?

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who is also in attendance, has previously said that he could be open to an apology, and the run up to the summit has been dominated by talk of apologies and potential financial reparations.

Both the king and the prime minister have spoken of using the summit as an opportunity to address future partnerships by devising approaches to tackle healthcare, education and climate protection needs among those "who struggle against ⁠hardship and disadvantage" rather than dwelling on the past.
"We cannot change the actions of those who came before us," said the monarch as he opened Tuesday's session, "We can, however, learn from the past."

Burnham has said he would like to discuss debt resets for smaller Commonwealth nations as well as announcing ⁠a €48.2 million ($54 million) investment into ​critical infrastructure in the Caribbean over the next three years.

blocks.caption: Despite calls for reparations, King Charles has emphasized building strong future partnerships within the Commonwealth rather than dwelling on the pastImage: Matias Delacroix/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What was the British Empire's role in the transatlantic slave trade?

The British joined the institutionalized slave trade in the seventeenth century, and quickly eclipsed other European powers before involvement in the trade was outlawed for British subjects in the Slave Trade Act of 1807 and then done away with in the wider British Empire in the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833.

During that time, Britain outfitted almost one-third of all transatlantic slave voyages, facilitating the forced transport of over 3.2 million Africans, mainly to British colonies in the Caribbean and North America.
The Commonwealth of Nations consists largely of former British colonies whose combined GDP of roughly $14.5 trillion accounts for about 15% of the global economy.
The Commonwealth in Africa: Real impact or empty promises?

articles.title: Seven flights across Europe targeted by suspected bomb threats
articles.summary: Planes in Poland, Spain, Bulgaria and Italy have been checked for explosives following separate threats.
articles.byline: Emer Moreau, Jaroslav Lukiv, Laura Gozzi

blocks.text: Seven passenger planes across Europe, two of which departed from the UK, have been inspected following a series of suspected bomb threats.

Two Ryanair flights, one originating from Dublin and the other from Lisbon, were searched after landing in Rome following anonymous tips but no explosives were found, sources at the city's Fiumicino airport told the BBC.
The Dublin flight was escorted by the Italian Air Force until landing. Authorities have also searched planes in Poland, Spain and Bulgaria.
While officially there is no link between them, authorities from various countries will be co-operating to assess whether this was a co-ordinated attack, designed to disrupt airspace.
The UK government described today's incidents as "malicious hoax threats".

In a statement it said it had "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we've seen today".
Aviation security expert Paul Mason said bomb threats on passenger planes "don't happen that frequently", which made the latest incidents "unusual".

"It sounds like they've been made in a credible manner across a broad range of airlines," Mason told BBC Radio 5 Live. "That would suggest to me that it's been a very deliberate act by a typical actor rather than a load of coincidental, malicious calls."
He said "there are a lot of processes" that the onboard crew and people on the ground must go through "to validate the credibility of the threat".

A flight may be asked to divert if the credibility of a threat "is of a certain level", Mason added, and in some cases the onboard crew may not even be advised on what the ground operators were dealing with.
In Rome, sources at Fiumicino airport told the BBC police bomb disposal experts carried out standard security protocols to ensure the safety of all passengers and crew.
Inspections of the passengers, luggage, and the aircraft yielded negative results, and the alert has since been cleared.
One plane which landed in Murcia, southern Spain - a Ryanair flight coming from Manchester - was also found not to have any explosives on board, Spanish authorities said.
One passenger later said she was unaware of the bomb threat until after the plane landed.
"We weren't told anything during the flight," Sarah told BBC Radio 5 Live. "The plane stopped quite suddenly and then we were kept on the runway for around 30 minutes."
"Then the fire engines turned up, the bomb squad turned up and we were asked to evacuate," she continues.

Sarah said the plane had not been on the ground a minute before it was "surrounded by fire engines and police and a bomb squad". All the passengers were then escorted by police, leaving all their belongings.
"We were only later told that it was an actual threat, a bomb threat to the plane itself," she added.
Two flights heading to Warsaw were also affected, including one from London Heathrow.
The Heathrow flight was originally meant to land at the Polish capital's main airport, Chopin, but was diverted instead to the smaller Modlin airport, briefly forcing its closure.
A Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw-Chopin landed as planned.
Later on Tuesday, Bulgarian Transport Minister Georgi Peev said there were bomb threats against two planes travelling to the country's capital Sofia.
He told the state-owned Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) the flights were from the northern Italian city of Bergamo and Ireland's capital Dublin.
The flights into Sofia were not diverted and no explosives were found when the planes were checked, Peev said.

Bulgaria's border police said in a statement sent to the BBC that at around 10:35 (08:35 GMT) it had received an email about "the presence of an improvised explosive device on a flight returning from Bergamo".
"Standard procedures for such incidents were immediately activated, and an operational headquarters comprising representatives of various institutions was convened," the statement said.
The border police added that the same email also reported a "similar threat against aircraft arriving from Dublin".
These incidents come a day after a Wizz Air flight from London Luton made an emergency landing in Budapest, escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet, after a bomb threat.
Wizz Air said later that security checks had been made and nothing was found.
BBC Verify has consulted aviation safety experts about what happens on board a plane when a bomb threat is issued.

Marco Chan, a former pilot for Cathay Pacific Airways and Hong Kong Airlines who is now a senior lecturer in aviation operations at Kingston University, said a bomb threat is considered "genuine until it is resolved, even though most turn out to be hoaxes".

Chan said crews will "quietly search" toilets, galleys and storage areas and will not touch a suspicious item unless it has to be taken to an area on the aircraft designated as the least risky bomb location.
The aircraft's captain will have multiple factors to assess, according to former airline pilot Terry Tozer, an aviation safety commentator.
He said these include what facilities are available at the airport they are being diverted to and how the plane can continue onwards should it turn out to be a false threat.
Chan added that once on the ground, the plane is generally "taken to an isolated stand, passengers are disembarked, and police and bomb disposal teams search it".

articles.title: The transplanted Scot doing famous father proud in New Zealand
articles.summary: Clark Laidlaw, head coach at Super Rugby champions Hurricanes, has made a huge impact in New Zealand and would "welcome a conversation" about taking on the top job in Scotland.

blocks.text: A few weeks back, four Scots shot the breeze in New Zealand, a meeting of rugby intellects transplanted from Edinburgh, Inverness, Yetholm and Jedburgh - all of them doing great things in their adopted land.
Mike Blair was one of them. On Saturday, in what promises to be a surreal day for him, the former Scotland captain will return to Murrayfield as attack coach for the All Blacks.
Euan Mackintosh was another. Mackintosh is the All Blacks' skills acquisition coach. The third man was Adam Hay, who is New Zealand's performance scientist.
The fourth was Clark Laidlaw, son of the great Roy, cousin of Greig and Super Rugby champion coach in 2026.
"We were getting a bit of stick at lunch, the four of us talking Scottish," says Laidlaw, whose Hurricanes team not only won Super Rugby in late June, they dominated it.

Finishing top of the table when the regular season ended, they won their first knockout game 66-12 against the Brumbies, then beat the Blues 57-21 in the semi-final before dismantling the Chiefs 60-5 in the final.
It was Laidlaw's third season in charge. He's far more celebrated in New Zealand than he is at home.

He's been there for 18 years, on and off, and he spoke about his life and times on the BBC's Scotland Rugby Podcast, how he went from a school-leaver at 16 to a New Zealand sevens coach - Commonwealth Games gold, World Cup Sevens gold, Olympics silver in Tokyo - to winning the ultimate club prize in southern hemisphere rugby in the summer.
Eight of Laidlaw's Hurricanes players are in Dave Rennie's touring squad and it might have been double figures had injury not taken a number of others out of the reckoning.
Laidlaw is a New Zealand passport holder now, but he'll be on Scotland's side on Saturday.
"You're gonna see New Zealand's strongest possible team, but there's no reason why Scotland can't win," he reckons. "It's been a bounce of the ball here and there [in recent games].
"Scotland are definitely knocking on the door. I want Scotland to beat the All Blacks and I want the All Blacks to win every other game."
He was 30 when he left Scotland for Taranaki, as a skills coach on the north island. Given his upbringing he always had a curiosity in him. His father always spoke about being a student of the game.
"I just thought there must be different ways to look at the game and different ways to look at life, really," he explains.
"I used to go and pass my rugby ball against a tree at lunchtime and train at night. I used to say to the old boys, I wasn't going to be staying here.
"They'd be like, 'Yeah, you'll be here'. I just knew I didn't want to be there for 20 years. It's not like I had a bad life in Scotland.
"I had a great job at East Lothian Council and I was coaching Jed-Forest. But I was curious to see what was outside of those big walls in Jed."

New Zealand has changed him, he says. Not just as a rugby man, but as a husband and father. The Maori and Pacific Island culture has influenced him in a substantial way, knocking some rough edges off his personality.
"Being around so many different people from different backgrounds took a little bit of my aggressive Scottish side off me," he says.
"Not too much, I hope. I have more empathy and more of an understanding side and I certainly didn't have that when I was younger."
That process started during his wildly successful years on the Sevens beat.
"The types of athletes we would bring in were often young, so it became an environment where we did have to look after each other," he says. "We had to look after young players.
"Mums and dads were sending their kids off to the Sevens. It was the first time they were leaving home. So we did have to have a caring element to that programme as well as driving them forward."
His time in New Zealand was interrupted by a brief spell at London Irish a decade ago. Around that time, he had opportunities to go to Leinster and Montpellier but he turned them down.
After two seasons, he was lured back to New Zealand - and his life really started to change.
All of this begs the question about his future. Is he a potential All Blacks head coach? Would he welcome a conversation about taking over from Gregor Townsend after the World Cup?
He thinks Kiwis are open-minded on coaches who they feel can help them win. Himself and Blair are proof of that.

The Scotland gig is more immediate, of course. "Gregor's done an amazing job," he answers. "Lots of coaches around the world will be looking at that job with real excitement for whenever Gregor moves on.
"I'd welcome a conversation. It would be a lot to up sticks and move back to Scotland, but you never know in sport.

"One thing I have learned is you can't plan. My focus is on the Hurricanes. If that leads to international rugby somewhere one day then I would definitely look at it, but looking too far ahead can trip you up."
He speaks about his dad, how proud he is of him and also of the pain of seeing him living with dementia.

In eight years as a Test player - courage and class in equal measure in the number nine jersey - Roy got 47 Scotland caps and four Lions caps. "That would be 120 games nowadays, wouldn't it," says his son.
"How is he? The short answer is he's doing as good as he can. He's safe and healthy. He's in a care home in Jed and is well looked after.
"The family is amazing. Greig's mum and dad are amazing. My middle brother lives close by and I feel for him because it's tough on him.
"John Rutherford and Keith Robertson [his fellow 1984 Grand Slam winners] go across every week and sit with him. It's one of the hardest things about being on this side of the world.
"It's always in the back of your head that Scotland is home and moving back at some stage might be an option."
Deep down, you hope Roy knows the heights his son has reached in the game and what a massive part he played in it all.
It's been some journey so far - and you sense there are many more adventures to come, at home or in his home from home.

articles.title: 3.4 magnitude earthquake near Esterhazy, Sask., likely caused by mining, Natural Resources Canada says
articles.summary: The earthquake — measured at a 3.4 magnitude — struck at 7:04 a.m. CST. Its epicentre was about nine kilometres east-northeast of Esterhazy, according to the NRC's Earthquake Canada website.

image.caption: The Mosaic Company's potash mine near Esterhazy, Sask. (Mosaic)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan
The earthquake — measured at a 3.4 magnitude — struck at 7:04 a.m. CST. Its epicentre was about nine kilometres east-northeast of Esterhazy, according to the NRC's Earthquake Canada website.
Mosaic Company operates potash mine in the area
An earthquake that shook homes and rattled people in the Esterhazy, Sask., area on Tuesday morning was likely caused by mining activity, according to Natural Resources Canada (NRCan).
The earthquake — measured at a 3.4 magnitude — struck at 7:04 a.m. CST. Its epicentre was about nine kilometres east-northeast of Esterhazy, according to the NRCan's Earthquake Canada website.
The federal agency says the earthquake was "a suspected mining-induced event," which is categorized as an anthropogenic — or human-caused — seismic event.
The Mosaic Company operates a potash mine about 15 kilometres northeast of Esterhazy.
Last year, the area was hit by three earthquakes, including two within three months. Earthquake Canada said those were also likely caused by mining activity.

Jason Whitby and his wife were just starting their morning when they felt Tuesday's earthquake. They heard a loud booming noise and their house shook, tipping over cups on the shelf and shifting art on the walls.
At first, he thought someone had hit their house.
"It was a crazy bang. It was a couple seconds then it was over," Whitby said in an interview with CBC. "I've never felt anything like that."
Whitby said he didn't feel the earthquakes that happened in the area last year, but he's concerned about damage to his home if the earthquakes become more frequent.
"It happens here and there, but nothing to this magnitude," Whitby said. "To shake a house is pretty crazy. It might get worse, too, who knows?"

items: 'The floor was rumbling': Earthquake confirmed in Esterhazy, Sask.

blocks.text: All Mosaic employees are accounted for and post-earthquake safety inspections are finished, the company said in a statement. About 1,200 people work below and above ground at the site, according to the Mosaic website.
Potash production was not interrupted and the earthquake happened "in a mined-out area of the older workings of the K3 Mine," according to the statement.
"Mining induced seismic activity in this area is common, and our facilities are engineered with seismic loading in mind," Mosaic said in the statement.

"While the recent event occurred far from current mining areas and presents no immediate safety concerns, we continue to advance our understanding of the geological properties of the K3 ore body and will work with external experts to review seismic activity."
The Mosaic Company operates the K3 Esterhazy mine. (CBC)
NRCan has recorded anthropogenic seismic activity in the Esterhazy area for decades, NRCan seismologist Claire Perry said.
"The number of natural earthquakes in this area is very low. It's not a tectonically active zone, far from active plate boundaries, far from the subduction zone," Perry said.

"So this is a stable region where we don't see a lot of earthquakes. And so we see these shallow events around Esterhazy, we know that they are related to industry activity and they've been going on for years."
NRCan has not yet received any reports of damage to houses or other structures.
Esterhazy Mayor Randy Bot said the town "is no stranger to seismic events" because of the mine's proximity.
"With one of the richest potash deposits beneath our feet, occasional ground movement is something our community has experienced over the years," Bot said in a statement to CBC.

"Our primary concern is always the safety of our residents and everyone working in the area. We have confidence in Mosaic and the monitoring, safety protocols, and regulatory oversight that are part of our mining industry."
The most significant seismic event in the area — with a magnitude of 4.1 — happened in 2019, but most measure in a range of 2.0 to 3.0 magnitude and only those above 2.8 are typically felt by people.
But Perry said it's still important to take precautions.
"Nothing is impossible and everyone should remember to be prepared and have an emergency kit ready," she said.

"Even if we don't live in an earthquake prone region … it's good to be prepared and know what to do should you feel shaking. The reflex should be to get under a desk or a table or something close by, take cover, protect your head and wait for that shaking to subside."

Potash mines excavate massive amounts of material from deep below the surface and create large cavities that can eventually shift or alter the rock strata above it, which in turn can create "cracking" or "fracturing" that produce seismic activity, said Andrew Frederiksen, a professor in the earth sciences department at the University of Manitoba.

"Even if you stopped all mining now, there are enough areas that were excavated already that this activity would likely continue," Frederiksen said. "Once you've got these open cavities from the mining, this kind of [seismic] activity is probably pretty inevitable."
The seismic activity is relatively safe compared to areas near tectonic faults and isn't indicative of future, larger earthquakes, he said.
"Something in the magnitude three or four range happening a couple of times a year is quite small potatoes on the global scale," Frederiksen said.
"The mechanism that produces these earthquakes [around the potash mine] has sort of a maximum size to it … whereas earthquakes caused by tectonic plate motions could scale up to be very large."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jeremy Warren is a reporter in Saskatoon. You can reach him at jeremy.warren@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Trump says US will end military aid to Israel by the end of this year
articles.summary:
US president makes surprise election day announcement, saying country does not ‘need’ $4bn annual payment

Donald Trump has said that the US will end military aid to Israel at the end of this…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has said that the US will end military aid to Israel at the end of this year in a surprise election day announcement that appeared to be targeted at voters sceptical of US support for Israel and the war in Gaza.
In a phone interview with Fox News as voting began on Tuesday morning, Trump said the US would cut nearly $4bn (£2.96bn) in military aid to Israel because “they don’t need it.”
“We were giving them $4bn … But it gets cut off at the end of the year,” he said.

Trump also indicated that he had decided to end the aid – which he claimed would be replaced by arms sales to Israel instead – because it had become a popular criticism of US foreign policy led by outspoken candidates including the Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” Trump said. “It’s a bad talking point.”

blocks.caption: Abdul El-Sayed, pictured campaigning on Monday, would become the US’s first Muslim senator if elected. Photograph: Zach D Roberts/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: During the interview, Trump claimed that the abrupt ending of aid was proposed by Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. “We give them $4bn of things and money, and they don’t need it,” he said. “And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”
Netanyahu had previously suggested tapering off US military aid to Israel over the next decade, but Trump’s announcement on Tuesday would significantly accelerate that timeline.

Israel received most of the approximately $3.8bn in 2025 as Foreign Military Financing grants that allow the country to buy US military hardware including F-35 fighter jets. Another $500m was given for joint missile defence programmes.

Trump’s announcement on Tuesday appeared timed to affect the outcome of the midterm elections, where US foreign policy and support for Israel have played an unusually important role in key races, including the Michigan senatorial race where El-Sayed is running against Republican Mike Rogers. He would become the country’s first Muslim senator if he is elected.
after newsletter promotion

A Quinnipiac University poll released in September showed that 48% of Americans believed that the US was too supportive of Israel, and other recent polls have shown a historic shift away from US support for Israel and Netanyahu’s government.

Anger over the humanitarian crisis in Gaza has helped usher in a wave of progressive Democratic candidates including El-Sayed, and Trump’s vice-president JD Vance has openly accused Israel of trying to sabotage US negotiations with Iran. In a June interview with the New York Times, Vance said of Israel’s foreign policy: “You can’t just kill your way out of solving every single national security problem that you have.”

During his Fox News interview, Trump spoke warmly about Netanyahu and also boasted about his own popularity in Israel. “If people ever got tired of me in the US, I’ll move to Israel and become prime minister,” he said.

articles.title: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
articles.summary: An engineer was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives, Binance says.

blocks.text: Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed.
Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign".

It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto.
Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened".
In a post on X, external, Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques.
These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, that can then be used to try and access their accounts.
Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives.
It said the perpetrators used "more advanced and deceptive" methods to build trust with him, such as sharing social media accounts that contained personal images.
The engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" during a second interview, that deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection.

Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and a compromised internal AI tool in October to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack.
The incident led Binance to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday.
Customers withdrew billions of dollars worth of assets after it reopened.
"We apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," it said.
The company added it had taken a range of steps following the incident, including working with law enforcement to trace and freeze affected assets.
It said it had also set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss, noting 98% of the token assets impacted had been "replenished" as of Saturday.
The record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) attack is thought to be the largest crypto hack to date.
US crime agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Secret Service, have been assisting Binance in tracing the crypto taken from the platform's own wallets.
The agencies, along with a range of cyber analysts, said that the hack - like similar breaches before it - bore the signs of having been orchestrated by North Korea.
Pyongyang hit back at the claims on Tuesday, denying it was behind the hack.

Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on the accusations were another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage North Korea's public image.
The country has consistently denied being behind a number of major cyber attacks it has been blamed for in recent years.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
Binance had previously not responded to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.

But on Tuesday, the company wrote in its post on X, external: "The latest information released by the Federal Bureau of Investigation indicates that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea is responsible for this incident."

As part of its security efforts following the attack, Binance said it would also increase investment in AI tools that can detect security threats, as well as engage third-party cyber experts to carry out a full-scale review of the incident.
It also said that it would seek to stablish a security research fund and work with leading AI and security firms on targeted initiatives.
